Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island.
  • The pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital.
  • The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

The pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

In a recent development, with no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

According to recent reports, “With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

The paddling portion went promptly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”.

It has been revealed that using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they said.

Sources indicate that mcDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Sources indicate that slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

Recent findings suggest that “One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We rapidly packed our boats and got on the water.”.

Industry observers note that in Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”.

#56351. Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long newly introduced route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m).
  • This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5.
  • Sources indicate that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long newly introduced route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to rapidly find a different goal.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

In a recent development, the team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us newly introduced hope,” Steadman recalled.

It has been revealed that off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman.

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”.

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” remarked Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”.

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart.

Industry observers note that “The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

It has been revealed that summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, “Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”.

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:.

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

According to recent reports, [We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, massive hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.
  • According to recent reports, the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

According to recent reports, the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

The small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot.

According to recent reports, macAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill claims, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

The spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot.

MacAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (360 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk.
  • It has been revealed that kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida.
  • Sources indicate that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

It has been revealed that kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Sources indicate that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His prepares expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards says, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

Adventure Links of the Week

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web.
  • It has been revealed that yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock.
  • A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

It has been revealed that yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Sources indicate that jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

According to recent reports, A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

According to recent reports, he Felt Stuck in New York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

Sources indicate that this Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Industry observers note that men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

According to recent reports, gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

#56342. Breaking: Food, so much food! (Day 166)

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (659 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Food, so much food! (Day 166)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s resupply day today!
  • We can never pass up a private pond beach though.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve talked about us rationing food and being hungry more often lately, but today I hit a newly introduced low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Follow Gerjan "Hungry" Hertgers.

Recent findings suggest that it’s resupply day today! We have 10 miles to go to Jo Mary road where Shaw’s will deliver our food drop. We have to be there before 2 pm, so let’s get going!

We can never pass up a private pond beach though. Even though the view is simply amazing, our attention went to an exploring ladybug. Climbing on top of a fire ring and us creating stick bridges to help her find the grass again. What more do you need for entertainment?

It has been revealed that I’ve talked about us rationing food and being hungry more often lately, but today I hit a newly introduced low. Just before the road crossing I got hit with a crazy dizzy spell and I had to sit down for a second. So this is what Dreamcatcher is usually experiencing, huh.

I’m hallucinating too. I swear I can smell a grill in the distance. My mind is playing tricks on me. Luckily, we hit the road and got our resupply! We can’t start eating like crazy though, since this resupply is just as tight as the last one. But luckily for us, my dad is here too! With sandwiches!! Score! I basically inhaled it before I could say any words. It’s good to see my dad again! But he didn’t look ready to hike. His knee is still bothering him too much. He made the hard decision to definitively get off trail and give up on reaching Katahdin. That’s a hard pill to swallow, for us both to be honest. But it’s the right decision. It’s just not worth it to cause your body irreparable harm for ego. I’m super proud of him. For getting this far, but also for making the hard but smart decision. He got a ride back to Shaw’s and will go to Millinocket soon. We’ll see him there in a couple of days.

Industry observers note that in the meantime we saw a sign: “Hot grill cold drinks across the bridge – Chilly P”. My nose wasn’t fooling me! There’s actually a trail angel in the middle of the 100-mile having a grill going!

It has been revealed that chilly P is awesome. He truly is super chill and grilled us an insane amount of burgers. I had four, on top of the sandwich I already ate. I would be lying if I mentioned I couldn’t eat more. There’s cold drinks, beers, fruit, snacks; basically everything a group of underfed hikers could ever need. It’s simply the best. We spent a good amount of time here, chilling with Chilly P.

After continuing, we came across a day hiker giving us some snacks. I guess our trail magic meter must have been full again! We’re so grateful.

At the end of the day, we reached a beautiful tent site on a peninsula on another lake, with mesmerizing skies. What a day.

Hi! My name is Gerjan. I'm a 28 year old Dutchman and I will be thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail (NOBO) with my dad in 2026! Besides crushing some miles every day, I will write up all about this journeys' beauty, struggles and everything in between for you to follow along and get a feeling for what it's really like out here.

#56341. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (953 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • Industry observers note that brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their plans to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

Industry observers note that brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

Indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

Another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She aims to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also plan to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

In a recent development, at least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 initiative is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

Industry observers note that if successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni says his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and initiative to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

It has been revealed that the Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a new route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Sources indicate that part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

It has been revealed that their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team plans a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

Industry observers note that the wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and proposal to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

#56338. A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (637 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Industry observers note that everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Industry observers note that everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” remarked Baia.

He says the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In a recent development, in addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health issues. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick new layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

According to recent reports, “Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

In a recent development, “Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

According to recent reports, that answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

In fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to proposal, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Industry observers note that everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin.

#56332. The Pulpit

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1682 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Pulpit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I score some candy, some great trail food, and get to offer some intergenerational guidance.
  • I accept Venmo, Cashapp, Zelle, Visa Gift Cards, and Guava candy read my last text to Pebbles.
  • It has been revealed that the spot wasn’t the quietest so I stayed in bed a little longer before propelling myself into the usual gamut of chores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a good day for my soul. I score some candy, some great trail food, and get to offer some intergenerational guidance.

I accept Venmo, Cashapp, Zelle, Visa Gift Cards, and Guava candy read my last text to Pebbles. Greasetrap was adamant that he come down to my van in the morning to collect the seating pad. I was glad I left it out for him when I heard some rustling outside my van 6:30AM as I was still a ways away from mobile. I could hear the windshield wiper move, and then what sounded like acorns being deposited nearby. I knew it must be my payment – guava candies!

It has been revealed that the spot wasn’t the quietest so I stayed in bed a little longer before propelling myself into the usual gamut of chores. I made my way out of the van and onto the trail around 8:00AM with my sights set on returning to The Pinnacle with an option to return to the Windsor Furnace Shelter if I had time.

In a recent development, the Appalachian Trail follows more high land between routes 183 and 61 for a long stretch all the way to the small town of Port Clinton. The south end the land drops rapidly, it would look like a ridge from below, but there is a wide flat area, unlike the narrow ridges that the trail has followed for much of the northern Pennsylvania section. A gravel road flanks the AT a short distance away, but I am saving that shortcut for tomorrow.

There weren’t any vistas along the trail, but there were some open areas along the way that provided some interest. The trail down to Port Clinton was a little challenging. It was aggressively steep and had the shape of a water slide, and it had about as much friction with a layer of leaves several inches deep. I had a few moments where it looked like I might slide all the way to the Schuykill River. Fortunately trekking poles are helpful to catch such slides.

Its hard to tell, but this is heading downhill in a hurry.

After doing my best to no recreate the scene in The Goonies where everyone slides down and ends up falling into a cave, I found that I had plunged straight into an active rail yard. The Reading Blue Mountain & Northern Railroad operates the rails here, and at least one locomotive was actively moving along the tracks. It took me a moment to figure out where to go, but soon I was making my way across the Schuykill River and into Port Clinton. The trail is only in town for a block before following the shore of the river then crossing under route 61. People seem to enjoy writing essays paragraphs long on the beams under the bridge. I didn’t have the kind of time to sit and read, but I did find one piece of artwork that I liked.

North of route 61 the trail climbs onto the next ridge which it follows a few miles before dropping in near the Windsor Furnace Shelter. I was figuring out my logistics for the rest of the day. I knew the spring at the shelter was dry, so I collected water from the creek fed by the reservoir up the hill. I hadn’t had any water since breakfast, so I planned to filter a liter at the shelter, then collect 2 more and carry them up to my camping spot at the Pinnacle. With my liter of water in tow, I approached the shelter to find a group of 5 (and a husky mix) having a picnic at the shelter. They were quite friendly and claimed to have “a lot of food” – music to my ears. Before I knew it a plate with a chicken wing and a cinnamon roll had been delivered to me, and a glass of white wine soon followed. Naturally I told the group about my hike and answered their questions while their husky constantly pursued whichever person of the group actively had a piece of food in their hand. I thanked the group for the early dinner, especially the fried chicken which really hit the spot. I found my way back to the creek, filled my water pouch up with 2 liters of water and waddled up the trail.

The Appalachian Trail meets the rail yard.

Crossing the Schuykill River in Port Clinton.

The AT follows the Schuykill River.

Who needs FarOut when you have a map this detailed?

A little food at the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

Recent findings suggest that the AT winds up for about two miles before arriving at Pulpit Rock, a vista that seemed like a smaller version of The Pinnacle. The extra time (well) spent at the Windsor Furnace Shelter meant that I probably was going to camp at The Pinnacle, I wouldn’t have time to go all the way there and get back before sundown. I figured it would be worth risking a wet tent with the chance of overnight rain to have a chance at another sunrise. I was closing in on The Pinnacle when I saw a trio of day hikers ahead. They looked considerably cleaner than me, but they were the kind of day-hikers that are eager to interact with us long distance hiker beasts. They asked if I was heading to The Pinnacle, and were using google maps to navigate. I think they felt that they would get there, but they were less confident in getting back to their car. The trail was much rockier and narrower than the easy dirt road north of the vista. One of them asked me if there was another trail to The Pinnacle. I confirmed that yes, the trail we were on continues. While I thought about whether that would be an easier way back to their car, I couldn’t help but add; “in fact, if you keep walking on this trail, you’ll end up in Maine. And if you turn around and follow it back the other direction, you’ll walk all the way to Georgia.” “What?! Did you guys hear that?” She called to her two companions, who were chatted a short distance behind us.

It has been revealed that I was quite pleased to have a few people to introduce to the Appalachian Trail. “Has anyone ever walked the whole thing?” was the first follow-up question. Yes! Thousands of people every year walk the entire trail. I replied. Many more questions followed, the group was happy to hear that the viewpoint was getting close, and very worth the walk through the rocks. I took over as navigator as we all scrambled across the rocks to get down to the best view.

Its rocky on this trail to The Pinnacle.

See You Tomorrow at The Pinnacle.

The three all seemed to be in their early 20s and anointed me their “trail dad” since I’d guided the group and shared my knowledge of the trail, including recommendations for their next visit. By now I knew that they would not be getting back to their car before dark. I had already confirmed that all 3 had fully charged phones so they could use the light of their flashlights to find their way back. I recommended that they take the road past the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society (LVAAS) observatory instead of the AT, it was shorter and safer to hike at night. After that they would be on easy state park trails the rest of the way. Everyone was pleased to have met me on the trail and eager to visit again. Maybe some day they will consider thru-hiking the whole trail.

It was now past sunset. I had hoped to spend more time finding a viewpoint at some angle I had missed the other day, but wasn’t successful. The rain forecast was looking rough for tomorrow, I had some regret about not joining the group on the way back and staying at the shelter. A little night hiking wouldn’t have hurt, I would miss any chance at a sunrise but I would definitely have a dry tent. I mulled all this over while eating my dinner. I considered a short night trek over to the rocky ledges before bed, but wound up falling asleep. I only made it to 8:00PM before waking up for the first time. I felt compelled to check out the night view, I was fairly certain there wouldn’t be much to see at sunrise and seeing the lights flickering off toward the horizon would make up for it a bit. I enjoyed checking out the night scene more than I thought I would, its something I’ll need to consider more often on future hikes – though that may need to wait until next year to come to realization.

Not a great picture, but I liked the night vibes looking far across Pennsylvania from The Pinnacle.

Total: 24.4 miles, 47,127 steps.

I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am upcoming to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

Latest Update: Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Confirmed

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been revealed.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush noted, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

According to recent reports, directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

Recent findings suggest that the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition unveiled Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Recent findings suggest that director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” remarked Kerry Stauffer.

Industry observers note that last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

It has been revealed that tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

Breaking: A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Recent findings suggest that rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Recent findings suggest that rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

Recent findings suggest that the first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

Recent findings suggest that from there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

Industry observers note that this is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka looks to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

#56325. Is There Ever a Case for Sleeping With Your Food While Backpacking?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (874 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Is There Ever a Case for Sleeping With Your Food While Backpacking?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve noticed that the thru-hiking community has a tendency to point the finger at day hikers and section hikers whenever there’s a debate about food and trash left out at campsites.
  • We all know the reasons you’re not supposed to: food attracts wildlife, and animals that get into people-food can come to associate campsites with an easy meal and start approaching people more often and more persistently.
  • In the case of small critters like rodents, this is annoying, possibly unsanitary, and can result in damaged gear and lost food supplies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve noticed that the thru-hiking community has a tendency to point the finger at day hikers and section hikers whenever there’s a debate about food and trash left out at campsites. “Thru-hikers aren’t the ones doing this” is the inevitable comment on any photo of a trashed campsite. That may even be true in many cases, but if there’s a food-related practice that many thru-hikers are guilty of, it’s sleeping with their food in their tents.

We all know the reasons you’re not supposed to: food attracts wildlife, and animals that get into people-food can come to associate campsites with an easy meal and start approaching people more often and more persistently.

In the case of small critters like rodents, this is annoying, possibly unsanitary, and can result in damaged gear and lost food supplies. In the case of large mammals like bears, it can lead to dangerous encounters, and food-conditioned bears may be relocated or killed as a result. Proper food storage is at least as much about protecting wildlife from people as it is about protecting people from wildlife.

Recent findings suggest that yet I can sympathize with the food-in-tent crowd: thru-hikers are always tired at the end of a long day, and proper food storage methods aren’t easy or automatic. Soft-sided bear-resistant bags like the Ursack can work well, but they’re expensive and somewhat heavy. Bear canisters are the most foolproof, but they’re heavy and inconvenient. Bear hangs require time, skill, and suitable trees to do properly, and they mean getting out of your warm bed to retrieve your food in the morning before breakfast. They’re arguably also more fallible than canisters and Ursacks.

In contrast, sleeping with your food is, well, easy. You don’t have to fuss with anything after dinner, you’ll have it right there with you if you wake up with a craving in the middle of the night, and you can make your morning coffee from the comfort of your sleeping bag.

It’s easy to imagine how, after weeks on trail with no food-related incidents, thru-hikers start getting comfortable with life in the mountains and start questioning whether all those cumbersome food storage steps are actually worth it.

So it begs the question: is there ever a case for sleeping with your food in the backcountry? Andrew Skurka has said that he does it on the regular, provided he’s camping in a low-use area where animals are unlikely to enter his camp and there are no specific food storage regulations there.

Beyond mere convenience, Skurka also argues that animals that have never become habituated to human presence tend to give us a wide berth, meaning food stored inside the tent might actually be safer than food stored outside.

Still, at a minimum, there are some circumstances where I’d say sleeping with your food is definitely a bad idea:.

I also want to add the caveat that “not sleeping with your food” should mean actually securing it somewhere else, e.g., in a bear canister. Not just leaving it lying on the ground outside your tent, which is the worst option of all.

Personally, I always store my food outside the tent, whether in a canister, Ursack, or bear/rodent hang. Even in low-risk areas, for me it’s simply not worth the small chance of a chewed-through tent, let alone a full-on bear encounter. Securing my food is a minor inconvenience that gives me more peace of mind, so I’ve just gotten used to it.

According to recent reports, is there a valid argument for sleeping with your food in some circumstances? Sure, but emphasis on some circumstances. For instance, a decent share of The Trek’s readers are Appalachian Trail people, and the AT is a prime example of a trail where I feel strongly that you should not sleep with your food. People do it even there, but “I sleep with my food and I’ve never had a problem!” is not empirical proof that a problem cannot happen.

Also, since fairly reliable food storage methods do exist, why not just use them and err on the side of keeping wildlife wild?

I’m not going to tell you all how to live your lives, but storing your food elsewhere is not the end of the world, and especially on a trail like the AT, it’s the more prudent choice for you and the bears.

#56324. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (417 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

First Ski Descent of Meru Central

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya.
  • Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.
  • “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

Industry observers note that the icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

Industry observers note that the icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

Industry observers note that at the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

According to recent reports, the skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

In a recent development, “We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

According to recent reports, tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

Industry observers note that in 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

In a recent development, it was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

In a recent development, “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

Sources indicate that inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

According to recent reports, “We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” noted local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

#56319. Industry News: Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar
