Industry News: Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • According to recent reports, today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

According to recent reports, today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

In a recent development, the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

It has been revealed that leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

There are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data reveals him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

Industry observers note that his article, cryptically titled Among the Massive Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

Recent findings suggest that A recent study indicated that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

It has been revealed that there is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

It has been revealed that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

In a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

Recent findings suggest that he continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

Industry observers note that it would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

Industry observers note that A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

Sources indicate that the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

Sources indicate that A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Sources indicate that if he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

According to recent reports, in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Industry observers note that chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

In a recent development, the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

Industry observers note that the three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Recent findings suggest that clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

In a recent development, he had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

According to recent reports, clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

In a recent development, if I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how substantial they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

Industry observers note that his 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

It has been revealed that clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

Sources indicate that one history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

Recent findings suggest that the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

In a recent development, the line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

It has been revealed that I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary Latest Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he shows to the world.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that some people dream of assembling a long-range rifle capable of ringing one-MOA targets at 1,000 yards. Others dream of an ultralight mountain rifle that’s easy to carry for miles and can make a single precision shot. I dream of an ultra-quiet, accurate, and handy rifle for dropping squirrels out of trees. Here’s how I turned a CZ 457 into my dream gun and how it performed in my testing this fall.

Sources indicate that the base rifle for this build is a CZ 457 American. I kept the American’s stock because I love a wood stock on a hunting rifle, and its ergonomics work great for squirrel hunting. There are a ton of ultralight chassis you can go with, but wood and squirrel hunting just go together. I did have to sand down the inside of the stock to create room for the new barrel, but that’s easy to do with a palm sander, a dowel wrapped in sandpaper, or every garage gunsmith’s favorite tool: a Dremel.

Read Next: CZ 457 American Review.

Lilja makes CZ 457 pre-fit barrels that are fantastic for competition shooting, but I wanted something lighter. That’s why I went with a 16-inch Proof Research pre-fit barrel. One of the great things about the CZ 457 is that the barrel changes are a piece of cake. You simply loosen two set screws to remove the barrel and the fresh one slides right into the action.

The entire Nightforce NX6 line is fantastic, and the 2-12x F1 variant is perfect for a versatile rimfire. It can take a 50-yard head shot on a squirrel or snap shoot one up close. It also makes this rifle excellent for shooting long range. Dialing in to 300 yards and ringing steel is quite easy with this setup. The scope is fairly light and short, so I don’t think I’m giving up much in terms of weight compared to a traditional 3-9x, but I’m gaining a lot of capability and versatility.

It has been revealed that this suppressor is quiet, light, relatively affordable, and easy to clean — everything I look for in a .22 can. There are plenty of other great options like the Dead Air RXD22Ti and the CAT BEN 22 Ti. A .22 silencer is a must-have accessory because it makes shooting a rimfire significantly more fun.

In a recent development, I added an Area 419 CZ 457 Scope Base and bolt handle to my 457 action. The rail makes it much easier to mount scopes and adds some elevation, so I can plink with this rifle out to 300 yards. The bolt handle makes running the bolt easier than the stock round one. One final upgrade I’d like to make is the Timney CZ 457 Trigger.

Sources indicate that for accuracy testing, I shot SK Rifle Match, Lapua Center X, and CCI Select. I shot five, five-shot groups with each. All three averaged around a 1/2-inch group at 50 yards. I was most impressed by how well this barrel shot CCI Select, which is relatively inexpensive compared to other ammo I shot.

The new barrel is definitely accurate, and it also made this rifle significantly easier to maneuver in the woods. With the rifle slung over my shoulder it was unobtrusive as I weaved my way through thick cover. When I saw a squirrel, the rifle came to my shoulder quickly and was easy to get stable.

Sources indicate that the result of this build is a rifle that’s fun to shoot on the range and a joy to carry in the woods. To me, it perfectly blends a nostalgic wood-stock rifle with modern features. Is it a bit extreme for a squirrel gun? You betcha. But I love this rifle all the same.

A Pleasantville Camino Day

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we officially started the three-stage Variante Espiritual of the Portuguese Camino.
  • Legend notes that after Saint James was decapitated in Jerusalem, his disciples placed his body in a stone boat.
  • Recent findings suggest that our apartment in Padrón had a full kitchen, so I started the morning by boiling half a dozen eggs and brewing a couple of cups of coffee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we officially started the three-stage Variante Espiritual of the Portuguese Camino. We had heard so many pilgrims rave about how magical this detour was, so we knew we couldn’t skip it.

Legend notes that after Saint James was decapitated in Jerusalem, his disciples placed his body in a stone boat. They crossed the Mediterranean and Atlantic, sailing up the Ulla River to Padrón before burying him in Santiago. Today, our journey took us in the opposite direction along that same historic Ulla River route—a short 2.5 km walk followed by a two-hour boat ride down the estuary.

Recent findings suggest that our apartment in Padrón had a full kitchen, so I started the morning by boiling half a dozen eggs and brewing a couple of cups of coffee. I sat out on the shared balcony, watching the sunrise over the misty Galician hills while letting Knockerz sleep in a bit longer.

Sources indicate that it was a cold, crisp morning when we finally set off at 9:00 AM. We strolled through the quiet streets of Padrón along the riverbank toward the docks, eager for the next leg of the adventure.

When we reached the boat dock, a boat roared up the river and unloaded 15 chilly pilgrims finishing their journey toward Santiago. To our surprise, Knockerz and I were the only ones boarding for the trip downriver. We had the entire boat to ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that as we entered the bay, hundreds of wooden platforms stretched across the water as far as the eye could see. The captain explained that these are bateas—floating mussel farms that drive a massive part of Galicia’s coastal economy.

There are around 2,000 of these platforms in the region, many passed down through generations from father to son. Each platform consists of heavy wooden beams with up to 500 ropes dangling 36 feet into the water. It takes about a year and a half for mussels to grow to market size on these ropes.

As we pulled into the harbor at Vilanova de Arousa, another group of 15 pilgrims was waiting to board for their trip up to Padrón.

Our accommodation was located right at the dock. This was our most expensive stay on the Camino so far—largely because options are limited in this beach town. But it was pure luxury:.

It was the ultimate “Nero” (nearly zero miles) afternoon.

We attempted to use the apartment’s washer/dryer combo, but after battling with European appliances and confusing instructions, we gave up and hand-washed our laundry in the sink instead.

In a recent development, later in the afternoon, we wandered into the old medieval section of town to look for food. Vilanova is a quiet coastal town; the local cathedral was closed, so we grabbed some groceries and headed back to cook dinner at the apartment.

We spent the rest of the evening sitting on the porch, watching local teenagers hang out along the waterfront as the cool evening breeze blew off the bay.

Up until now, we hadn’t had any luck finding English entertainment on the TVs along the trail. But when we turned on the TV in the living room, we discovered the previous guest had left their Netflix account logged in—and set to English! Having not watched a movie or TV show in weeks, we sat spellbound watching the movie Pleasantville. Given how relaxing and peaceful the day was, the title felt strangely fitting.

According to recent reports, by 9:00 PM, exhaustion caught up with us. Even though the summer sun wouldn’t set for another hour, we rolled down the heavy exterior window shutters, turned the bedroom pitch-black, and fell into a deep, pleasant sleep.

After decades of no backpacking an abrupt life incident forced me back into the woods for some shinrin-yoku where I ran into a NOBO tramily at Shuckstack Fire Tower. That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

#56312. Industry News: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1400 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • Sources indicate that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • According to recent reports, grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent newly introduced route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

Sources indicate that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman said. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two new routes with Blake Berghoff.

According to recent reports, grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he noted.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

In a recent development, the unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

According to recent reports, one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman says this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

According to recent reports, approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

Industry observers note that “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

Recent findings suggest that “Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

In a recent development, the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

It has been revealed that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Recent findings suggest that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment issues, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

It has been revealed that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he mentioned. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, the climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

Industry observers note that the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

In a recent development, route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

Recent findings suggest that the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman stated.

They then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

Descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The newly introduced 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#56308. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1077 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • It has been revealed that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

It has been revealed that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an vital figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up aims for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

Recent findings suggest that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

It has been revealed that though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Industry observers note that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

According to recent reports, the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

According to recent reports, attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

Recent findings suggest that the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

In a recent development, the few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

In a recent development, despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” notes Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

Sources indicate that the columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Sources indicate that essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

According to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In a recent development, in terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

According to recent reports, there have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

#56305. Latest Update: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (653 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio.
  • In a recent development, “I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan.
  • Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio. The property, which is owned by a family friend, has rolling hills and steep hardwoods and is scattered with hayfields.

In a recent development, “I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan. “I found good deer sign, with lots of buck rubs on trees.”.

Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait. Instead, when the season opened, he just walked the woods, scouting and hunting different locations. He used a lightweight tree saddle and climbing sticks to check areas quickly and quietly.

“I sat in six different trees over 12 hunts, moving according to wind and weather conditions,” notes the 26-year-old, who works in heavy construction.

On the morning of Nov. 7, he hunted a pinch point where he knew a few does were bedded.

“But I didn’t like the place and started walking the farm again when I climbed down that morning.”.

According to recent reports, it was the first cold day of autumn, cloudy and with temperatures around 40 degrees. Talbott located a couple of fresh scrapes, and climbed into a nearby tree around 1:30 p.m. to hunt that afternoon. He didn’t see much until about 4:30. That’s when he spotted a substantial deer headed his way along the field edge.

“I knew he was significant, and a shooter, and it all happened very fast.”.

When the buck stepped behind some brush 15 yards from Talbott, he drew. The deer stepped into an opening, and Talbott released his arrow.

Talbott saw the deer run about 30 yards and, pouring blood, enter the timber toward a distant hayfield. Then it disappeared over a hill.

According to recent reports, “I was shaking uncontrollably when I called my wife, dad, and best friend [Brady Garren] and told them what had happened,” Talbott says. “Dad and Brady got there after sunset to help me look.”.

Carrying flashlights, the three men followed a blood trail for about 150 yards. But the trail petered out. Then they heard thrashing in a nearby ravine. Thinking it might be Talbott’s buck, they backed out and called in Triple BC Deer Drone Recovery for assistance.

“They got there with a drone a couple hours later,” says Talbott. “They flew the drone to where we last found blood and in just a minute the buck was found in the ravine, but its head was up.”.

It has been revealed that they waited an hour and flew the drone again but saw just a slight movement from the buck. An hour later when they flew the drone a third and final time, they saw the buck was dead.

By then, around 11:30 p.m., more friends had arrived and seven people went into the ravine to help haul out Talbott’s huge buck.

“I knew he was a great buck, but I had no idea he was that big until I walked up to him,” Talbott says. “I was beyond ecstatic.”.

Recent findings suggest that it was after midnight by the time they field dressed the buck and dragged it 600 yards to the truck. They loaded it and drove to a friend’s cooler.

According to recent reports, the next day Talbott’s wife, Alison, took photos before they caped the buck and processed the meat. The buck has 16 points and is an estimated 5.5 years old.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

Recent findings suggest that “My taxidermist says it should score about 190 inches,” says Talbott. “The whole thing is so unreal I can’t explain how I feel. I spent a lot of time there hunting and learning the farm, how to use the wind and where the deer were bedding and scraping … It’s just an incredible experience.”.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

Industry observers note that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Sources indicate that vasiliev remarked that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Sources indicate that baia claims the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

In a recent development, on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no fresh soft snow had accumulated.

According to recent reports, the Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#56301. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1308 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • In a recent development, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In a recent development, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin said. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Industry observers note that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

According to recent reports, this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

In a recent development, for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

It has been revealed that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

Sources indicate that if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

According to recent reports, the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

In a recent development, once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

According to recent reports, thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Industry observers note that that stated, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

It has been revealed that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

According to recent reports, once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the significant cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Sources indicate that ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Recent findings suggest that conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

Sources indicate that in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that “That is why it is crucial to consider all options and potential concerns before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

It has been revealed that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they stated. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

It has been revealed that they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.
