General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • Recent findings suggest that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

Recent findings suggest that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

Recent findings suggest that A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

Industry observers note that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

It has been revealed that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police mentioned the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

According to recent reports, avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident demonstrates that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

In a recent development, the accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

The avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Sources indicate that fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the substantial powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) highlights low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

In a recent development, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps demonstrates remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

#56249. Hiding Out in Town With a Whole Bunch of Hikers

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2065 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Hiding Out in Town With a Whole Bunch of Hikers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this morning I woke up pretty dang early at the room in Strawberry.
  • Sources indicate that the town of Strawberry is a smaller town just down the road from the town of Pine.
  • Recent findings suggest that kitty Hawk wound up calling Al to confirm the details and told Al that there were about 8 of us who would be interested in going to be breakfast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this morning I woke up pretty dang early at the room in Strawberry. Which was a little bit of a challenge, because there were 5 other hikers in the same room! I got up slowly and as quietly as I could and headed into the living room. I put my contacts in, combed through my hair, and brushed my teeth. Slide and I weren’t the only ones up though. Woods was walking around in the kitchen and starting up a pot of coffee. The rain was pouring down outside, and I’d spent much of the evening listening to the roar of thunder. What a perfect day to spend in town! It wasn’t long before hikers began waking up and heading into the living room. I think someone put a movie on first thing, because what else is there to do? Then we began to scheme about breakfast.

Sources indicate that the town of Strawberry is a smaller town just down the road from the town of Pine. There is a breakfast joint in Pine, but the breakfast place in Strawberry is unfortunately closed today. Apparently yesterday this larger group of hikers met a local guy named Al and his wife. He had mentioned that he would come by this morning around 9AM and pick people up to go to breakfast in town. Slide and I were both very intrigued, but we weren’t a part of that original strategy whatsoever. I figured since there were 10 hikers in the house, it was probably pretty unlikely that there would be enough room in the car for all of us to go to breakfast.

Recent findings suggest that kitty Hawk wound up calling Al to confirm the details and told Al that there were about 8 of us who would be interested in going to be breakfast. And what felt like a lost cause to me turned into yet another trail miracle. Al stated that it was no problem for him and his wife to drive separately to pick us up, that way there would be enough room for all 8 of us in the cars! It was a rainy-day miracle. I was absolutely ravenous at this point, so it was very good news. Since we got into town so late last night, we weren’t able to stop at the store or pick anything up. Which meant I woke up this morning wildly hungry.

The server gave our table two massive, hot cinnamon rolls for free before our food even came out.

According to recent reports, around 9AM the large group of us left the Airbnb and walked down the road to a parking area with a bunch of mailboxes. That was the easiest place for Al to pick us up, and we didn’t mind the short walk. Al and his wife were incredibly nice, and we hung out at the parking lot talking with them for a bit. Then they drove us into Pine and all of us sat to eat at the diner in town. The staff was incredibly nice and were able to seat all of us at one big table. They even brought us over hot, fresh cinnamon rolls to eat while we waited for our food, on the house! I wound up getting a breakfast burrito with chorizo and Dr. Pepper. I didn’t get my soda fix last night so I couldn’t resist the call, even at breakfast.

From left to right: Lazarus, Woods, Leaf, Al & his wife, Kitty Hawk, PI, Slide, me, and 9 Lives.

While we sat there another AZT hiker wound up coming into the restaurant and she joined us. Her name was Mel and she was also staying in town to wait out the storm. Apparently, there were at least a couple other hikers in town as well that she had seen. Everybody ate and then sat around talking at the table for a long time. It was really nice to catch up with 9 Lives, who I haven’t seen in person since we were hiking the CDT together in 2024. We hiked around 2,000 miles together that year and it doesn’t feel possible that it’s been so long. The other hikers at breakfast were Lazarus, PI, Kitty Hawk, Woods, Leaf, Slide, Al, his wife, and me. As we sat inside, we got to watch the rain pour down outside. That is always incredibly satisfying when you’re on trail. It feels like a huge win to make it to town and be able to avoid bad weather.

Free mini pies from the diner in Pine.

Recent findings suggest that after everyone finished eating, we got ready to head out. But not before the lovely staff at the diner gave us about 6 mini pies to take home with us. They were a day or so old but still looked incredible. Then once everyone paid, we decided to walk across the street to a Hippie Shop, just for fun. They had clothing, accessories, and all sorts of random stuff. I didn’t find anything that spoke to me but Slide wound up finding a button-down shirt that he really liked. It was just fun shopping around with no place to be. Then before we headed back to the Airbnb, Al drove us to the grocery store to grab a few things there. I grabbed some drinks and random things there but didn’t get too much stuff. We’re actually planning to check into a separate room later on today and I don’t want to have to carry a bunch of stuff around.

Industry observers note that the Airbnb that everyone is staying at is absolutely perfect, but it is filled to the brim with hikers! Last night it was completely full, and someone was sleeping on the couch. And while we were at the breakfast place we ran into Torin aka Espresso, another hiker that we last saw at the North Rim. He was looking for a place to stay tonight too and decided to come with all of us back to the Airbnb. Since we’re going to be in town for 2 more nights it just made more sense to book another place down the street and be a little more comfortable. I’m hoping to get a bunch of writing and editing done which will be easier with some more space. The blueprint for now is to just hang out with everyone at the Airbnb until around 3PM. Then Slide and I will go and check in to this other spot just down the street. That way we can still hang out with everyone but also enjoy a bit more space.

The AZT sobo hiker bubble waiting out a storm in Strawberry, AZ.

Once everyone finished grocery shopping, we got a ride back to the Airbnb with Al. And not long after we got inside it began to pour like crazy outside. It even hailed for a while! Everyone got comfortable back at the Airbnb and put on another movie. We all sat on the couch, talked, and enjoyed the show. I even got some editing done while we all hung out. Then just before 3PM I got a notification that we could go and check in at the room down the road. There was a break in the rain which felt like the perfect opportunity. I just wanted to drop everything off before the weather started up again. Then we would probably come back to the Airbnb to hang out with the gang later on.

In a recent development, the hippie shop in Pine was adorable and really fun to walk around. They even gave you these cute reusable bags with any purchase.

The place that I booked for the night was called the Strawberry Inn, and it was really adorable. The location had a bunch of tiny home style rentals which were perfect for us. Plus, I was even able to book a room that had its own private hot tub. The idea of soaking in a hot tub while it rained sounded amazing. The room was perfect for the two of us and had everything that we could need. We got comfortable there and I decided to get some of my electronics charged. Then I went through my food bag to access how much more food I might need for this next stretch. I had even seen online that there was a Walmart nearby which would deliver. So that was going to be my plan to get the rest of my resupply goodies at some point.

The big group of hikers hanging out outside of the hippie store in Pine.

It has been revealed that not long after we checked into the room, we were already hungry again. Luckily this location was right around the corner from the couple of different restaurants in town. At this point it was raining lightly but it wasn’t too terrible. So, we just carried our umbrellas and walked the short ways down the road to the bar and grill that was open. When we walked inside there was absolutely no indication that the place served food. The bar was full of guests, but nobody was eating. But they did indeed sell hot food! I wound up getting a chicken sandwich with a side of fried cheese curds. Those are really delicious. I also got a Dr. Pepper, but it had a really weird flavor likely due to coming from the bar soda gun. It was the strangest tasting Dr. Pepper that I’d ever had.

A chicken sandwich with a side of fried cheese curds!

Slide and I hung out there for a bit and enjoyed our food. Then retreated back to the Strawberry Inn to relax for a while. I got some more editing done and Slide went through his photos. Then later on we decided to walk back over to the Airbnb to hang out with all of the other hikers. They were still watching yet another movie when we arrived. Truly though, what else is there to do in this town? We joined them for another one and wound up hanging out until sometime after 9PM.

One of the only joints open in the town of Strawberry.

It has been revealed that eventually we decided to walk back down the road to our room for the night. There is actually a breakfast place right next to the Inn which is going to be open tomorrow morning. It was closed today and the menu looks really good, so I’m excited to try that out tomorrow. We’re going to be taking our second zero day in a row tomorrow to wait out worse weather. Apparently, the rain is supposed to be much worse tomorrow than it was today, and more than an inch and a half of rain is expected over the course of the day. I’m looking forward to another day of rest and having some more time to get my writing and video editing done before we hit the trail once more.

If you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The adorable tiny home at the Strawberry Inn that we’ll be staying in the next 2 nights.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the SOLGW Mk 1 made waves last year for rising to the top during a grueling selection process in which one of our Tier One SOCOM units selected to field it.
  • Not surprisingly, it has since become one of the most desirable AR-platform rifles in the commercial market, though many would-be buyers have balked at its hefty price, which is just shy of three grand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that the SOLGW Mk 1 made waves last year for rising to the top during a grueling selection process in which one of our Tier One SOCOM units selected to field it. This 11.5-inch carbine chambered in 5.56 NATO demonstrated the best reliability and performance among its peers.

Not surprisingly, it has since become one of the most desirable AR-platform rifles in the commercial market, though many would-be buyers have balked at its hefty price, which is just shy of three grand.

I’ve spent the last several months running the carbine to see whether the juice is worth the squeeze and you can see it in action in the video here.

It has been revealed that my experience with the SOLGW Mk1 has been universally positive. I’ve run it in several configurations, in terms of the optics I’ve mounted on it and with respect to the types of muzzle devices I’ve employed. In all cases, the rifle has run without any glitches.

More impressively, my hands-on time with the rifle has shown how it rises to the occasion when called on to perform different tasks.

It has been revealed that for instance, in a multi-gun capacity I ran it with a Vortex 1-10 Gen III Razor LPVO and a Holosun 507C in an offset Area 419 mount. Not only did this setup perform well at distance with the LPVO at 10X, but I was able to quickly transition between far and near targets by rotating the rifle 45 degrees to bring the Holosun’s halo-style reticle rapidly into view.

In a recent development, in another configuration, I ran the rifle with an EOTech holographic sight and 3x magnifier paired with Unity FAST mounts and EOTech’s OGL weapon-mounted laser and IR designator. This setup is much closer to how SOCOM assaulters kit-out the gun. Unsurprisingly, the rifle worked like a charm here too.

Recent findings suggest that A final thing worth noting is the primary muzzle device I used is the Huxwrx Flow 556 Ti, which is also similar to the military’s selection for the Mk1. The rifle has a non-adjustable gas block that balances extremely well with this suppressor, and cuts the gas going back into the shooter’s face to basically zero.

In conjunction with the bolt-carrier group and buffer system, the gas block and suppressor, enhance the SOLGW Mk1’s reliability and soften the recoil impulse in a way that makes the rifle very easy to control.

Reports from the operators who field the rifle indicate that its lethality, performance and reliability are outstanding.

Based on all this, it looks like the Mk 1 delivers in a way that justifies its price, and then some.

#56244. Are Deer Dogs Really the Problem with Deer Hunting in the South?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2078 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Are Deer Dogs Really the Problem with Deer Hunting in the South?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, past an old logging gate, a gravel road snakes through a young stand of pine.
  • In a recent development, limestone Creek is just one camp within a patchwork of clubs that are scattered around the Pearl River region of south-central Mississippi.
  • On this morning Orders arrives last, in typical fashion, with his blueticks and beagles in tow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, past an old logging gate, a gravel road snakes through a young stand of pine. Meandering through the stand, my truck headlights brighten the back wall of a squat tin building that looks more like an old feed shed than a deer camp. Inside, a makeshift counter holds a logbook for stand locations and check-ins. An aerial map of the property (all 3,000 acres of it) and faded grip-n-grin photos of bucks from past seasons adorn the walls. Every member of the Limestone Creek Hunting Club lives within 20 minutes of here, so there’s no need for actual living quarters. Before this camp house was built, members like my grandfather and father just gathered around an old burn barrel that marked the official rendezvous point. They would meet there first, then decide where to turn the dogs out each morning of the season.

In a recent development, limestone Creek is just one camp within a patchwork of clubs that are scattered around the Pearl River region of south-central Mississippi. And while a few other surrounding camps also hunt deer with dogs, the Limestone club has clung to this tradition tighter than any, for almost 50 years. In that half century, their dog hunts have become something of an art. The preferred mediums are CB radios, beagles, and old lever guns or pump-action rifles. The featured artist behind these runs is Tim Orders, one of Limestone’s longest tenured members.

On this morning Orders arrives last, in typical fashion, with his blueticks and beagles in tow. While collaring the dogs, he directs everyone to specific posts; road crossings, food plots, and creek bottoms, all named after hunters or the bucks they’d killed there. And while the Limestone club has taken plenty of significant bucks over the years, antlers aren’t the reason its members keep coming back. The club’s history,  the shared excitement on successful hunts, and the enduring camp traditions are what dog hunts are really all about.

Recent findings suggest that but for deer hunters who don’t use dogs, and aren’t part of the tradition, it’s easy to be skeptical when you see a battalion of orange vests spread along the roads—possibly near your hunting property. While there are plenty of deer dog hunters who understand boundaries and sensible hunting etiquette, there are plenty who don’t. Those who don’t will surely run through some treestand hunter’s setups. Hunting deer with dogs is currently legal in nine southern states (MS, LA, AR, NC, SC, TN, GA, VA, FL), and when the hounds get to barking it can feel like the end of deer season for everyone else.

But just because dog hunting season begins doesn’t mean that treestand hunters should give up. Here’s what all hunters should understand about dog hunting, and how they can adapt their strategies to still be successful once the hounds hit the woods.

I hunt several areas, both public and private, where deer dog hunters frequent. This year, I rode shotgun with Orders during one of his club’s first hunts of the season to see his deer dog strategies and to learn how to adapt my own hunting around dog hunters. If you’re unfamiliar with hunting deer with dogs, here’s an overview:.

It has been revealed that if your only experience with deer dogs involves a pack of beagles running through your treestand setup, you probably aren’t a fan of the tradition in general. I’ve been on this end of a dog hunt several times. It can be frustrating. You wake up super early, get to your stand before daylight, only to have a spike run through after sunrise with a pack of beagles trailing behind. It will feel like that spot is burned for the day.

But if you understand how deer react to dogs, you can still be successful during dog season even if you’re not with the deer dog crew.

In a recent development, my grandfather killed his three biggest bucks with dogs in the woods. Two of the three were taken during still hunts when dog hunters on neighboring properties ran deer onto the private ground he was hunting. He’d hunted with dogs before, so he knew the neighbors might run a buck by him.

I know several other hunters who look at dog season as an opportunity to give their hunting season a spark. Land Smathers is a dedicated Mississippi deer hunter who consistently kills mature bucks during dog season, often on public land.

It has been revealed that smathers cited one instance when he noticed that a party of dog hunters convened near some public ground he planned to hunt that morning. His familiarity with this particular ground gave him an idea of where the hunters would likely turn the dogs out, so he decided to swiftly set up where he anticipated dogs might drive the deer.

“I knew that area, and there was only one place the deer could go if they were bedded there,” he said. “I slipped down a ridge that dumps into a river bottom where the deer would have to travel or cross the river. Once the dogs cut a track, deer started to funnel through this natural pinch point. I watched several does and a couple small bucks trot through the bottom until a shooter emerged. He came through at 60 yards before I leveled him with a shotgun. The dog hunters weren’t mad that I’d shot him, but they didn’t help me drag him out either.”.

Smathers he didn’t always take advantage of dog season throughout his hunting career.

Sources indicate that “It used to bother me,” he stated. “I’d see a bunch of trucks with dog boxes at the store, and I would turn right around and go home. I finally realized that sulking about it didn’t do any good, so I just learned how to hunt around them, and it’s paid off a few times.”.

Recent findings suggest that smathers’ experience and success in the middle of dog season has made him more empathetic toward the practice, and he sees more hunting opportunities, even with dogs, as a good thing for hunting overall. A lot of hunters grumble that deer hunting with dogs ruins the rest of their season or burns their best spots. It can certainly take a few days for things to return to “normal” in areas that dogs have covered, which is more problematic if you’re hunting small private properties. But the truth is, deer dogs don’t often drive deer completely out of an area.

“We only run dogs during the second season, which typically aligns with our rut,” Orders indicates. “It seems contrary to most hunters, but that time of year, deer can be so unpredictable anyway. We’ll turn the dogs out in spots where we know a buck is bedded, and if we don’t kill him right away, we’ll give that spot a rest and get a trail cam pic of him back in that same area within a couple days, if not sooner.”.

Orders noted that this is especially true during the lockdown phase of the rut, or if there’s a hot doe in the area.

Industry observers note that “If the dogs split up a buck and doe, he’ll return shortly to find her again,” Orders notes. He also isn’t surprised when a new buck shows up on the property during dog season.

Orders’ style of dog hunting allows him and his club to jump bedded deer that have been heavily pressured. These bucks likely wouldn’t be caught moving during daylight hours otherwise. It’s logical to think that pressure from dogs might make bucks even more nocturnal. But this hasn’t been the case for Smathers, who spends about half his time hunting public land that gets hammered by dog hunters every season. In fact, many of his mature bucks were taken during dog season or shortly after it. Like Orders, he’s noticed that most of the time, bucks will show up shortly after the dogs are gone. While these mature bucks might not daylight in the middle of a food plot, they’re still moving, just in thicker cover, Smathers says.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to join a deer dog club to get in on the action. If you’re hunting public ground, and you decide to stick it out when the dog hunters roll up, make sure you’re at a safe distance from other hunters and wearing blaze orange. Then, follow these tips.

It has been revealed that hunt from the ground. If there was ever a time to ditch your treestand or saddle, it’s now. Being stuck in a tree limits your chances of getting a shot. But if you’re hunting from the ground, you can rapidly change position as needed.

It has been revealed that cover likely escape routes. Deer prefer the path of least resistance. This is especially true with dogs on their trail. Deer will typically follow their preferred travel routes when jumped. But instead of bed-to-food travel, focus on bed-to-bed travel. The deer are headed for more cover, what’s the quickest route for them? That’s where you need to setup.

Use terrain features. You can use natural pinch points like saddles, creek or river crossings, and ridge systems to your advantage. You can find these with OnX or HuntStand and then fine-tune your setup once you’re there in person. Approach these areas similarly to how you would treestand hunt them but with more flexibility for your setup.

Play the wind. Even though they move based on where the dogs bump them, you can bet deer, especially mature bucks, will still use the wind to their favor. If you’re upwind of the deer, you’re unlikely to get a shot before they detect you.

Hunt the backdoor. Dog hunting crews often refer to an unlikely or underrated travel route that as the “backdoor.” Mature bucks love to sneak out through the backdoor. If you’re hunting a neighboring property and hear the dogs running parallel or even away from you, don’t leave just yet. If a mature buck is bedded near other deer that the dogs jump, they’ll often hang tight until the commotion passes and then slip out opposite or perpendicular to the rest of the deer to head for different cover. If possible, position yourself between “the backdoor” and the next potential bedding area.

Just get out there. If you already adhere to the “you can’t kill them from the couch” approach, this also applies during deer dog season. Adapting your hunting strategy is always a better strategy than sitting at home. And if you’re lucky, it might end with a buck heading straight for your setup.

The day I joined Orders for one of Limestone’s hunts, the dogs jumped several does, but no one shot. While Orders isn’t against shooting does this time of year, especially for first timers, there’s an understanding that the club prefers to hold out for bucks. Even though no tags were punched, I still got to hear the dogs bark see all the action of a hunt well run.

READ NEXT: The Vanishing Legacy of Southern Rabbit Hunting.

Sources indicate that the next day, Orders and his crew did tag a buck and the shot several more before the season ended. With just 14 days (minus a few for bad weather) Limestone’s success rates are a thing to admire, especially when you consider that they only run half days. The club imposes a strict 12 p.m. deadline on itself, as opposed to conducting all day runs like a lot of other hunters might. Letting the property rest is key to their success, which is just one of the many lessons they’ve learned through years of running dogs. One of the key tenets that Orders and his son follow is to drop everything in order to catch dogs before they chase deer off the property. This philosophy not only leaves the club in good standing with surrounding clubs and landowners, it’s even helped them land a few extra spots to run.

Unfortunately, not all deer dog hunters hold themselves to this standard, and most of us can only watch while howling beagles run deer through our setups. But like any hunt, adapting is often the key to finding success. So the next time you hear the dogs jump a deer in your area, stick it out. A big buck could be headed your way.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police confirmed that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun.
  • Recent findings suggest that his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment.
  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Sources indicate that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police confirmed that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

Recent findings suggest that his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

In a recent development, ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#56241. Breaking: Double Zero Days During More Arizona Trail Rain & Flash Flooding

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1950 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Double Zero Days During More Arizona Trail Rain & Flash Flooding

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This morning I actually slept in pretty late at our room in Strawberry.
  • Grabbing breakfast from the farm stand place in Strawberry.
  • When we got over there a handful of hikers was hanging out and ordering some more food.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning I actually slept in pretty late at our room in Strawberry. It was nice knowing that there was no pressure to go anywhere or do anything. My only goals for the day are to get some editing done, eat a bunch of food, and resupply for this next stretch of trail. By the time that I did finally get up, Slide was very ready to eat. So, we decided to get our rain gear on and walk down the road to the breakfast farm stand right by the Strawberry Inn. I checked the hiker group chat and saw that a group of hikers from the Airbnb had walked over there and was hiding out from the rain in some kind of a shed. The place pretty much only has outdoor seating, but apparently the staff revealed the hikers where they could hide out and eat at the same time.

Grabbing breakfast from the farm stand place in Strawberry.

When we got over there a handful of hikers was hanging out and ordering some more food. We got in line and ordered some stuff to take back and eat at our room, since it was right down the road. Everyone else finished up and wound up going back to their Airbnb to hang out. I figure we’ll head over there at some point today. But I also have a mountain of editing to get done, and it will definitely be easier to do it somewhere quiet. My eyes were way bigger than my stomach this morning, so I wound up ordering two things. The first was a lemon ricotta pancake, which sounded absolutely divine. And I also got a breakfast burrito to eat later on, just in case. On trail I always feel like I order way too much food or not nearly enough. Which is likely why I usually wind up ordering way too much.

The farm stand breakfast spot in Strawberry, AZ served one of the most incredible pancakes that I’d ever had.

Industry observers note that we took the food to go and brought it back to the Strawberry Inn to eat and relax. And that lemon ricotta pancake was one of the best things that I’d ever had. I love ricotta but have never had it in a pancake before! Prior to getting on trail I was cooking a lot at home and making a ton of homemade pizza. Oftentimes I would top it with ricotta because it is so delicious. But this just opened my eyes to a whole fresh use for the stuff. I didn’t wind up eating everything right away but figured I’d just graze on it for the next couple of hours.

It has been revealed that after I ate, I decided to get right into business and start doing some writing and video editing. I also had an exciting call with a brand that I’ve worked with in the past and am going to be working with next year. My looks for 2027 are finally starting to come together and I’m really excited to be able to share it with you all eventually. The tiny home that we were staying in had a separate room which was pretty much the size of a walk-in closet. That was the perfect place to do some audio recordings and get certain work done for a while. Once all of that was done, I could get the rest of the work done more comfortably, while also watching a little bit of TV.

Recent findings suggest that in the afternoon I also had to place a Walmart delivery order to the inn. I had a lot of food, but definitely not enough to be comfortable for the next 71 miles. Our initiative is to hike out of town and continue 71 miles to the next highway crossing, where we can go into the larger town of Payson. That will be about 3 days of hiking including the day out of town, and I’ve had a massive appetite lately. It also sounded nice to get some drinks and snacks to enjoy this evening while we were at it. Before I placed the order, I messaged the hiker group chat to see if anyone needed anything random. Hikers always do! And sure, enough one hiker needed some sunblock and things like that. Which was easy enough to add on to the order. Plus, we’re going to be getting a ride back to trail tomorrow with a few of these hikers, so we’ll be seeing them.

Recent findings suggest that figuring out that you can do things in small towns such as place an online food order to be delivered is certainly a thru hiking hack. I had never even thought about doing anything like that prior to hiking the CYTC last year. Time was my most valuable resource and I was willing to do a lot to save it when I could. Oftentimes you’ll spend an hour walking to a store in town, resupplying, and then perhaps another hour walking back to the room. Some trail towns are spread out with miles between all of the essential locations. Oftentimes stores like Walmart won’t even charge a delivery fee for orders if you spend over a certain amount. Today I’m grateful to be able to do this and not have to hitch into the town of Pine to go back to the grocery store. Then hitch back once we’re finished.

While the Walmart order got delivered, I got a bunch more editing work done. I’ve also been sending a lot of emails and setting plans into motion for my upcoming hike next year. It feels a bit like Deja vu, honestly. When I was hiking the CDT in 2024, I did the bulk of all of my planning for the following years border to border CYTC hike. There are so many logistics involved in a hike like that. Plus, you need a lot of gear! I remember dedicating serious time in towns to do video editing and also all of that coordinating back then on the CDT. Then when I finished up the hike I went home and had about 6 weeks to finish all of the planning and work as much as I could to save up money for the endeavor. I guess this is just the season for it. But this all feels very familiar.

This wound up being the perfect space to spend a couple of days off in town. I got most of my work done in that little room by the couch. And there is another bed on the other side of that wall.

According to recent reports, eventually our Walmart order got delivered, but not without minor issue. The driver had some trouble finding the place, which I was expecting. The address for our location was pretty confusing. But then after the groceries were delivered, I noticed an item that we hadn’t ordered. Then I realized we were missing a few things that we had ordered. Luckily, they were all drinks, so it wasn’t anything essential to us getting back out on trail. But they were sugary drinks that I was excited to enjoy. There isn’t any kind of a store or gas station in Strawberry, which is really the only thing that this town is missing. My favorite thing to do in town is to buy a bunch of different beverages and drink them all over the course of the day. Typically, on a double zero such as this, I would probably have bought a small case of soda or something like that. Liquid calories are my secret to not losing too much weight on trail.

By now the day was already starting to wrap up. Zero days on trail have such a miraculous way of slipping right through your fingers. It happens every single time without a doubt. At least I did get a lot of “work” done today and I also felt like I relaxed a lot. There really isn’t anywhere to go in this town, so there was no reason to be anywhere except for the room all day. A little after 5PM we started figuring out what to do for dinner. Everyone at the Airbnb had gotten so many groceries that they were just going to be staying in and trying to eat through everything. I wasn’t starving at this point, but I knew that later on I would be. Over the course of the day, I ate the rest of my lemon ricotta pancake and the whole breakfast burrito. That little farm stand in Strawberry was fantastic.

Surprisingly our options for dinner this evening were not limited. There were actually a few places open in town tonight because it was later in the week. One place sold empanadas, but they actually did wind up closing right before we were ordering food. Then there was also a steakhouse and an Italian restaurant. We wound up getting a massive white sauce pizza to split for dinner and were able to just walk down the road and pick it up. It was hardly raining at this point, though it had rained heavily for most of the day. It was pretty nice out when we walked to grab the pizza. The moon is incredibly full right now which is exciting moving into this next section of trail. I love night hiking when the moon is full.

It has been revealed that once we picked up the pizza we retreated back to the room for the rest of the night. The gang was just over at the Airbnb watching a movie. And while it would have been nice to hang out with everyone, I wasn’t in the mood to walk another mile just to watch a movie somewhere when I could just stay in bed and watch a movie there. It was too easy. The pizza was delicious and just what I needed. After we ate, I was contemplating going in the hot tub again. I went in this morning after breakfast and it was wonderful. But I think that going in first thing tomorrow will be even better. After eating I just relaxed for the rest of the night. I got a little bit more writing done and we watched TV for a while. Then I did my stretching routine and laid up on my phone for longer than I should have before finally calling it a night.

Industry News: Air Rifles Are Still Underrated for Substantial Game Hunting. Here’s Why They Shouldn’t Be Overlooked

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Eventually, a growing number of airgun manufacturers released larger caliber and more powerful rifles to market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that I lived in Europe for several years and was introduced to quality airguns for competitive shooting and hunting while there. In the late 90’s I obtained my first PCP rifles, a .177 Daystate Huntsman followed by a .22 Webley Raider. It did not take long to appreciate the advantages these guns offered for small game hunting. When I returned home I found there was a small but enthusiastic community of airgun hunters testing the limits of the existing technology.

Eventually, a growing number of airgun manufacturers released larger caliber and more powerful rifles to market. It was only a matter of time before we started to think about using air rifles for larger game like deer and hogs. It was about this time that I first heard of Dennis Quackenbush and the substantial bore airguns he was producing, initially in .308 and .50 calibers, but eventually the .457 became his flagship model. I purchased the .308 in early 2002 for predator hunting, using it to bag fox and coyote. About the same time the idea of using these rifles for larger game really took hold with me. But why would anyone want to use an airgun, rather than a conventional firearm?

In a recent development, quite simply, because it’s fun, challenging, and effective. In the following overview, I’ll give a brief history of the massive bore airgun, the motivations for hunting with them, the power they are capable of generating, hunting regulations, ammunition used for hunting, and how to keep the rifle filled with air and ready to hunt.

There are several advantages to airguns in general: they are safer to use in more developed and densely populated areas, they are far quieter than even a rimfire, and ammunition is less expensive. But in my opinion these advantages are less significant when discussing large caliber rifles. Why use them then? For many it comes down to the challenge of the hunt, the requirement for the hunter to exercise the discipline to get closer, be more selective in choosing the shot, and be more precise in shot placement. At least for me, hunting is more about how you do it, than just the outcome. Many hunters find this challenge through hunting with handguns, archery, or muzzleloaders.

In this respect hunting with a big bore airgun is closer to the ethos and field craft of bowhunting but based on the core skill set of the rifleman. And this is what many enjoy most about hunting big game with an airgun, it forces a hunter to close the range and be very precise in shot selection, with the discipline to work for the optimal shot and hold back until that is achieved.

According to recent reports, the first commercially available rifles that were applicable for larger quarry, were the Quackenbush big bores. With the advent of this upcoming generation of big bores, the power outputs that could be achieved with an airgun jumped from the 30-40 foot-pound of energy (fpe) range obtained with a standard .22 to over 400 fpe. And just like that, the potential for using them on deer or other large game became a reality.

Industry observers note that if like me, you grew up hearing that a deer rifle needs to generate over 1,000 fpe to be effective, this 400 number seems very low. Well, It turns out the 1,000 fpe threshold is simply wrong. I have killed many hogs with airguns generating 100 fpe, and hogs are harder to kill than deer, in my opinion. And many times, when hunting alongside others using centerfires, my kills have been cleaner and more decisive. This is because I get in closer and place the shot more precisely. The best air rifles produce a wound similar to an arrow in that there is no hydrostatic shock generated, but rather direct injury to the vital organs. The simple fact is that 300 fpe is plenty of power to kill deer-sized game but you have to be selective with your shooting and be capable of hitting your target. You cannot be a sloppy or lazy in airgun hunting.

Today’s big bore airguns can be very powerful, and there is a wide selection of calibers and power outputs to choose from. An key factor to understand, is that the caliber is only one element contributing to the power an air rifle can generate. A .50 caliber slug in one rifle design may generate 250 fpe, but that same slug in another design can produce more than 800 fpe. The power is defined by the gun, the pressure it charges to, the pressure and volume of air it releases, and the efficiency of air flow and the guns valving system.

Sources indicate that when talking about the more powerful rifles such as the Hatsan Piledriver, Umarex Hammer, Air Force Texan, and Western Bushbuck, you should expect to get over 600 fpe in a .457 and over 700 in the .50 caliber versions. One of the newer players in the major bore space is the AEA Zeus, which is a .72 caliber that comes in various barrel lengths and can generate between 1,000 fpe to 1,500 fpe.

Getting the rifle optimized for a hunting application is a balancing act between power, accuracy, and shot count. Some major bore airguns are regulated, for instance the Umarex Hammer has a factory set regulator adjusted to operate at 3,000 psi, and since every shot uses the same air pressure and volume it is very consistent. Some rifles, such as the AirForce Texan allow the user to adjust the power, which is usually achieved by increasing or decreasing the tension on the hammer spring. And others, such as the Western Bushbuck, have a two-step cocking position that allows either a full power or reduced power shot to be achieved. In many ways, a power adjustment on an airgun is an analog to hand loading for a powder burner.

Read Next: The Most Powerful Airguns.

Initially, the problem big bore airgunners faced was finding game that could be legally taken with their guns. Regulations were the barrier, and in the early days there were very few places that allowed airguns to be used for anything other than small game and pest control. Most jurisdictions have separate deer seasons for firearms, muzzleloaders, and archery that are very specific in defining the criteria for each method. And up until a few years ago, none of them specifically allowed airguns for big game. But there were a few workarounds, Texas for instance did not allow any (big or small) game animal to be taken with an airgun. However non-game species such as feral hogs, predators, and exotic species, could be taken in any number, at any time, and by any means.

Texas became ground zero for early significant game airgun hunting in the U.S. The state has large populations of feral hogs, and there are also populations of feral Spanish goats, axis deer, and aoudad that could be hunted. I started flying down to the Texas to meet up with my buddy Eric Henderson, and we would roam the state hunting hogs and exotics during the day, then go after predators at night, with our Quackenbush air rifles.

Recent findings suggest that we experimented with our guns, trying different fill pressures and hammer springs, to optimize power, accuracy, consistency, and the highest shot count. Somewhere along the way, big bore airguns gained visibility and more people started shooting them. This led to grassroot movements lobbying state wildlife management authorities to introduce provisions for airgun hunting, and newly introduced regulations came on the books.

In a recent development, at the time of this writing, several states including Michigan, Indiana, Alabama, Missouri, Georgia, Virginia, Tennessee, Kentucky, Idaho, North Dakota, and a growing number of others allow deer hunting with substantial bore airguns (airgun hunting law resource). Texas and Arizona not only allow deer to be taken with airguns, but most other species of big game can be taken with air powered PCP rifles as well. Some states place a caliber and/or power restriction on the guns that are permitted, so you need to check local regulations. Under these upcoming regulations, airguns have taken whitetail and mule deer, elk, bison, bear, mountain lion, javalina, and pronghorn.

Along with the North American hunts, I’ve been traveling to South Africa for almost two decades to hunt plains game with air rifles, after being granted permission to do the first sanctioned airgun hunts there in 2003. Many of my significant bores have been used to take kudu, wildebeest, blesbok, impala, springbok, warthog, bushbuck, and several other species over the years.

Many of the manufacturers producing substantial bore airguns offer ammunition as well. These may be produced inhouse or on an OEM basis, but in general there is a wide selection of ammo available in all big bore airgun calibers (.308-.72). Hatsan offers their own line of big bore “pellets” in .457 and .50 caliber in a variety of weights. Not surprisingly, they work very well in the Hatsan guns. Established muzzleloader companies such as Hunters Supply have an extensive line of big bore airgun slugs and pellets as well, and even the heavy hitters like Nosler have stepped in with a line of airgun ammo.

One of the companies whose product I use a lot is Mr. Hollowpoint, which is a small operation run by Robert Vogel. He was one of the early substantial bore airgunners and knows airguns inside and out. The slugs he produces are mostly (but not all) hollow points that are specifically designed around the individual guns.

Sources indicate that airguns can be notoriously finicky about the ammo they prefer, and even guns out of the same manufacturing run might have different preferences. When I get a upcoming rifle, I will try a few slug configurations and weights until I find the one that’s most accurate—then I stick with it. Of course, if you want to use a flatter shooting 86-grain .308 slug for coyote and switch to a heavier 126-grain for better penetration on feral hogs, that’s fine. You just need to find pellets in both weights that work for your gun and commit to those.

In a recent development, here’s another key consideration for all air rifle hunters: How will you keep the rifle filled? There are a couple options, but in my experience a handpump is not a viable one. The volume of air a big bore requires, the high pressures they usually fill to, and the high-volume air usage all make a handpump ineffective. This leaves you with either getting an air tank that you have filled at a paintball or dive shop, or getting your own compressor.

Tanks are a good approach; you will want to opt for a large-volume carbon fiber tank that can be filled to 4,500 psi. These tanks are connected to the rifles on board storage using a high-pressure hose with either a female quick release connector or a proprietary fill probe. The air flow circuit is opened so that the air flows from the high-pressure tank to the low-pressure onboard storage, and when the gun reaches the required pressure, the tank’s valve is closed, the bleed valve opened, the gun disconnected, and you are ready to go.

Tanks are moderately priced, fast and easy to operate, and are probably the most convenient means of filling a rifle. There is a downside though, first you need to find a place with a compressor that will fill your tanks (look for paintball shops or dive shops, which will usually do this for a fee). A bigger problem is that these shops are often unable or unwilling to charge the tank up to 4,500 psi.

Another option, especially for a high-pressure high-volume rifle is to get a portable compressor. Up until a few years ago this was cost prohibitive, unless you shot a lot or had a group of shooters going in together, as a compressor could easily cost more than $3,500. But there are several compressors (both AC and DC models) on the market today that can fill an individual gun to a 4500 psi, and they can cost less than a carbon fiber tank. The downside is they take longer to charge the gun than a tank does, they are loud, and they require some upkeep. Personally, my preference is to have both a CF tank and a portable compressor to use in combination, using the tank to charge as high as its residual pressure will allow, then topping off with the compressor.

Each of the topics we’ve covered could fill multiple chapters on their own, but now you have an honest overview major game hunting with an air rifle.

I quit hunting with anything but air-powered guns almost 15 years ago, but before that I had moved to handgun hunting and bowhunting to increase the challenge. The airgun is an effective, efficient, and ethical method of take for deer and other substantial game, but you need to use the gun appropriately. If you just want to go out and shoot a deer at long range and call it a season, a big bore airgun is probably not a good fit for you. However, if you want the challenge of closing the range and dropping the slug precisely on target, you need to give hunting with an air rifle a try. Now more than ever, big bore airguns are readily available. There’s a broad selection of models with a range of features and price points, and there are more places to hunt with them than ever before.

#56237. How to Shoot a Shotgun (and Hit Every Bird) Like Your Granddaddy Did

How to Shoot a Shotgun (and Hit Every Bird) Like Your Granddaddy Did

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Don Zutz, 43, has hunted and fished all his life and has won or scored high in many skeet and trap tournaments.
  • Sources indicate that harry couldn’t understand it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Don Zutz, 43, has hunted and fished all his life and has won or scored high in many skeet and trap tournaments. He was the 1964 Wisconsin skeet co-champion in 12 gauge with 100 straight and shot 150 straight in the shootoff. This story was originally published in the November 1976 issue of Outdoor Life.

Sources indicate that harry couldn’t understand it. He was a lifelong duck hunter and had never had any trouble hitting his share of waterfowl. His season birds-to-shells-fired average was quite impressive. That very morning, in fact, I had watched him drop a lone honker and a pair of passing mallards with only four shots. And on previous occasions when he forsook his beloved blinds for pheasant hunting, he had more than held his own.

According to recent reports, but Harry’s bubble burst when I suggested that we switch to open-bored guns and visit a few grouse covers after our early-morning duck hunt. It was a fresh world for him. Three roaring flushes from grouse netted him only half a dozen empty shells to reload. Then he missed a spiraling woodcock. Harry was beside himself with frustration and embarrassment.

“How can I be deadly at dawn and then turn into a flub by midday?” he growled.

At first I didn’t pay attention. Anyone can have a bad day on grouse. When he continued to growl about his troubles over a hot cup of coffee, however, the reason for his bad showing became obvious.

According to recent reports, “I guess those fantails are just too fast and tricky for me,” he mused. “When ducks and geese come over, I’ve got plenty of time to measure off my lead, but I simply can’t get ahead of these crazy grouse and swing with them—especially when they’re twisting through the brush!”.

Anyone who is conversant with the various wing-gunning methods immediately realizes that Harry had been using the wrong technique in the thickets. Instead of building his lead with a fast swing, he had used the deliberate, precise method of leading that he had perfected during all those years of dedicated duck hunting. And because it had also worked well on pheasants in the open, Harry had never questioned his method. For him, a carefully held sustained lead was the way to go. It was his one and only wingshooting technique.

But deliberate shotgun pointing doesn’t work on fast-breaking game in thick cover. The hunter simply cannot measure off a precise lead and maintain it on a grouse that is threading its way through branches. Harry found out that a versatile wingshot selectively employs different methods of leading flying targets, depending on what he is shooting.

There are four basic techniques for slapping a lead on speeding birds, clay or feathered: 1) the sustained lead, otherwise known as the maintained lead; 2) the swing-through method, alias the fast swing; 3) the pull-ahead system; and 4) the snap shot (see sketches).

The one Harry had been perfecting in duck blinds, lo those many seasons, was the sustained lead. This is the method called “maintained lead” by the late, great D. Lee Braun, an outstanding Remington skeet and trap pro, in his popular book “Skeet Shooting with D. Lee Braun.”.

According to recent reports, the shooter visualizes the amount of lead he will need for a given target flying at a given speed and then brings his gun up ahead of the target by that approximate distance. Swinging at about the target’s speed, he then adjusts for the exact lead and continues swinging on the bird’s apparent line of flight until he is satisfied that the alignment and forward allowance are perfectly correct. The trigger is pulled while the gun maintains the established lead and swing speed. If the shooter judges his lead correctly, and if he maintains his lead and swing speed by following through properly, he should center his birds.

The sustained lead, like all the others, is subject to human error. The shooter who gets lazy during his swing will slow down unwittingly and shoot behind. Ditto for the gunner who tries being too precise, because any tendency to aim a scattergun like a rifle results in tightening up, which also slows the swing. The most common failing, however, is stopping the swing at trigger time, thus cancelling out the forward allowance.

Recent findings suggest that many hunters miss with the sustained-lead method because they don’t measure off enough lead. In other words, they overestimate shot-string speed. Even at skeet’s meager 20-yard range, the low-house target at Station 3 and the high-house clay at Station 5 (right-angle-birds) require a full four-foot lead if you use this method. Passing ducks doing 70 feet per second at 40 yards require an 8½-foot lead, even with a high-velocity load of 4’s doing 1,330 feet per second at the muzzle. Stretch that range to 60 yards, and the lead increases to 14 feet! In other words, you might visualize a rowboat between the duck and your shotgun’s muzzle while also keeping the swing crisp and smooth at the duck’s speed!

A sustained lead is best employed in the open on targets flying a steady course. It is natural when hunting doves, ducks, and geese, firing at crossing skeet clays, and for certain pheasant-hunting situations.

Recent findings suggest that but the sustained lead can’t be used effectively in the brush on fast-flushing birds. There isn’t enough time, and the game seldom flies a steady course. I pointed this out to Harry.

“Guess I’ll have to start snap shooting, if I want some grouse,” he said.

I didn’t like that idea either, and tried to dissuade him. Snap shooting is the least-scientific and least-consistent shotgun technique. It consists of nothing more than picking a spot ahead of the moving target, pointing the muzzle at that spot, and firing. There is no swing; there is no attempt to coordinate with the target’s speed; there is no follow-through. The gun is merely snapped, or poked, and it is virtually stationary, when the shot charge is triggered. If the shooter “guesstimates” right, he scores. Otherwise it’s a miss. And misses always outnumber the hits.

Recent findings suggest that this is not to say that snap shooting doesn’t play a role in modern wingshooting. When a hunter is caught completely off guard and can’t recover in time to make a coordinated swing, his only chance lies in a snap shot.

In my opinion, about the only time snap shooting is really best is when you are trying for cottontails in the brambles. Those bounding, zigzagging, change-of-pace artists seldom allow you to take a smooth swing, and a hunter must resort to the “poke-and-hope” method. (For very different opinions on snap shooting, see Robert W. Woodruff on quail in “Five Topflight Gunners Tell How” in the October 1976 glitch of this magazine, and Peter Miller on woodcock on page 72 of this issue.).

In a recent development, many skeet and trap shooters use a variation of snap shooting that they call spot shooting. This specialized technique has arisen because most clay-target shooters already have their guns mounted and pointed at a specific spot when the claybird appears. They do not have to bring their guns to their shoulders from a low, field-carry position. In trap, the first bird of doubles is often spot shot, because the shooters know exactly where it will be. Many skeetmen “spot” the high-house bird at Station 1 and the low-house disc at Station 7. But since a hunter doesn’t walk around with a mounted gun, and since he doesn’t know when or where the birds will appear or how they will fly, spot shooting has little application afield.

“I’d sooner see you try the swing-through method,” I told Harry. “It’s more dependable and consistent, and once you get the timing right, it can be lightning quick. In fact, some people call it the fast swing instead of the swing-through.”.

“Well, right now I’ll try anything,” Harry muttered, spinning the cap back onto his thermos.

I explained that the shooter starts his gun behind the target. He then swings aggressively, catches up with the bird, and strokes right through it with a muzzle speed faster than the target’s flight. The mental command to fire is given just as the muzzle passes the moving mark, and the gun continues its accelerating swing along the target’s line of flight.

Theoretically, the correct lead is built up by the rapidly swinging gun while the shooter’s muscles respond to the mental command to fire and while the trigger yields, the firing pin falls, the primer ignites, the powder burns, and the shot charge clears the barrel. The faster the swing, the longer the lead will be. The muzzle moves ahead of the target during the shooter’s physical responses and the gun’s lock and combustion time.

According to recent reports, the swing-through system can be applied to more different hunting, skeet, and trap situations than any other method. I’ve even come to favor it over sustained lead for distant birds, because the accelerating, “heave-ho” swing needed to generate leads of eight to 15 feet after coming from behind develops a gun momentum which, in turn, insures a good, positive follow-through.

In a recent development, unfortunately, however, some people can’t handle the true swing-through method. They don’t feel comfortable starting behind the bird. They are doubtful about swinging with gusto, and lack the timing needed to coordinate trigger pull with swinging muzzle.

Sources indicate that harry was one of them. After years of starting his gun ahead of ducks and geese and taking a deliberate, measured lead, he didn’t like swinging from behind and firing with no visually apparent lead.

But there was still hope. The following weekend I had him try a variation called the pull-ahead method. With this technique the hunter starts by bringing his gun up right on the bird. Then he builds up gun momentum by pulling ahead for a very short distance. Once he has gun alignment and momentum, the shooter moves the muzzle ahead of the bird. When the right amount of daylight appears between muzzle and bird, the trigger is pulled while the swing continues to accelerate. The amount of visual lead is supplemented by the time that elapses during the shooter’s body responses, the function of the gun, and the shot bore travel.

The pull-ahead method does require good timing. There is only one point during the accelerating swing when the muzzle is in correct juxtaposition to the target. In general, though, the average person masters the pull-ahead faster than he does the swifter movement required by the true swing-through.

Although the pull-ahead method hasn’t received much publicity, I’m certain many shotgunners use it unwittingly while thinking that they are employing the true swing-through. Thousands of skeet and trap shooters align directly on their clays first and then generate leads merely by swinging crisply ahead. The business portion of their swings never starts behind the targets, and yet many of them think they are swinging through. There’s nothing wrong with that, of course, but I believe a shooter should try to understand exactly what he is doing, not what he thinks he’s doing!

According to recent reports, in the field, pull-ahead shooting works nicely with incoming birds and close-range shots at upland birds. It also works well with rabbits when the cover is fairly open. This method is faster than sustained lead, less complex than the swing-through, and more dependable than snap shooting.

Read Next: How to Miss Fewer Birds.

Industry observers note that harry picked it up easily. He felt comfortable coming up with the muzzle on the bird rather than behind it, and he liked seeing daylight between barrel and bird. But he knew better than to look for a precise, measured lead. He still uses the sustained lead for ducks because there is more time and open sky. In the brush, he found, it is simply a matter of getting on target, swinging ahead briskly, and letting go with a positive follow-through.

This doesn’t mean pulling ahead can be used for all kinds of shooting. I seriously doubt that its abbreviated swing, starting on the bird, can develop enough gun momentum to generate the really long leads needed for distant crossing shots at waterfowl.

To be a versatile wingshot, the scattergunner must have more than a single swing/lead system in his repertoire. He should learn the strengths and weaknesses of all four basic techniques, practice them with claybirds until the movements are automatic, and then apply the appropriate method as field conditions and individual shots dictate. There is no other way to become a successful all-around performer with the bird gun.

  • It’s hard to believe in late December we are still talking early ice, but in the Midwest unseasonable warmer temperatures have kept water open.
  • Safety is an important consideration for any sort of fishing, especially early ice.
  • In most cases, ice anglers like to be mobile, drilling holes in the ice until they find fish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s hard to believe in late December we are still talking early ice, but in the Midwest unseasonable warmer temperatures have kept water open. Northern Minnesota and North Dakota, however, are experiencing some excellent early ice walleye fishing and the remainder of the Midwest shouldn’t be too far behind, so get those batteries charged and hooks sharpened because ice fishing season is coming. Here are 10 tips that will help you land more walleyes as lakes begin to freeze.

Safety is an important consideration for any sort of fishing, especially early ice. Never venture out without letting someone know where you are going. A good spud bar is paramount for testing the ice but any heavy stick will work. Place your cell phone in a plastic bag, carry a rope along and invest in a reliable ice axe in case you should fall through.

In most cases, ice anglers like to be mobile, drilling holes in the ice until they find fish. That’s not necessarily a bad practice at the right times, such as mid-day or slow bite periods. However, use your fall fishing as a form of scouting. If you found good weed beds and break lines near shore in September and October, target those same areas the first few days and weeks of ice fishing.

You need to be stealthy when fishing early ice, because fish may very well be shallow or on the move as they transition into the coldest water temperatures of the year. There are a lot of new noises, from footsteps to augers, and ATVs coming from above, making these walleye a bit more cautious than usual. Move quietly and minimize noise especially during peak hours such as early morning and evening. Do your best not to move when the fish are moving. As the sun begins to set, you should already have your holes drilled and be fishing at or relatively close to where you expect the fish to be, come evening. Being set up for the fish before they arrive is key to not spooking them out of the area.

In a recent development, bait size is often overlooked by many ice anglers. But it’s pretty simple. Bigger bait means bigger fish. If you are targeting panfish, make sure you are using small baits such as tungsten jigs and small waxies. If you are targeting eater size walleye, you can often get by with a fathead minnow or shiner on a jig, mid-size spoons, and glide baits will put those walleye onto the ice as well. For trophy walleye don’t be afraid to rig up creek chub, red-tails, and larger profile baits such as Rippin’ Shads, Rippin’ Raps, and many of the other lipless style baits. When the bite gets tough, downsize your baits and minimize expectations. Everyday isn’t a trophy walleye day.

Tip-ups have been around for as long as I can remember and they are a great way to cover water and maximize the number of baits you can legally have out. I prefer to fight the fish on a rod and reel versus the old hand lining method. With all the innovations in ice fishing rods, it is easier now than ever. Placing your rod in a rod holder (known as dead-sticking) is extremely effective and many will tell you that their bigger fish came on these setups. A dead-stick rod allows you to see the bite easier. The rod loads up and in many cases will set the hook for you instead of letting the fish swim around freely while getting tangled up in other lines. And when it comes to fighting substantial fish, you are more likely to land them on a rod and reel combo as opposed to hand-lining a lunker top side. No transducer is needed in the hole of your dead-stick, which minimizes noise and why many believe bigger fish are more likely to bite.

According to recent reports, lively bait can be a challenge when you’re fishing in arctic temperatures. But with all the innovations in insulated and aerated bait stations keeping your water moving and bait highly oxygenated they will remain as lively as they were when you purchased them. It’s usually the angler’s fault for not having lively bait. The cold water temperatures create more viscosity in the water, which means everything moves slower. This is why an active bait can attract a fish to bite from a long distance versus a dead minnow hanging below the ice. Shiners, fatheads, and red-tails are all excellent live baits for ice fishing based on your location. Red-tails are a favorite among Minnesota anglers whereas shiners and fathead minnows, work just about anywhere. Creek chubs are the go to in the Dakotas and when kept fresh and alive they are some of the most active live baits under the ice sure to entice a hungry walleye.

Shorelines are a great starting point during early ice. Most shorelines hold structures such as weeds, rocks, and sand, as well as warmer water initially, making for a great starting point. As the day progresses, look for deeper water nearby such as main lake points and breaks. If you can find a location with a break fairly close to shore this can be the ticket as you won’t need to move a lot throughout the day and you’ll be in the perfect position for when those active walleye move up shallow to feed again.

Weeds hold fish all year long, because they create oxygen, which attracts everything in the food chain. Finding good weeds late in the winter is tough, but early ice weed opportunities can be the ticket. The use of a good underwater camera to do some mid-day scouting for weeds can pay dividends come evening.

Just like your bait, you need the right setup for the technique you strategy on fishing. A soft tip and longer rod can make for a great dead stick. But you will want a more medium to heavy powered extra fast action rod for larger baits when targeting those trophy walleye. The fast action tip will ensure quicker and more solid hook set. A medium action rod will give your bait the proper action when worked vertically through a hole as well as more control over that tanker walleye to guide it up through the narrow ice opening. The right rod will increase your hookups and your ability to land the fish. The wrong rod will increase your odds of missing bites and weak hook sets resulting in lost fish. When your rod is too soft and the action is too slow it’s very difficult to get a good hook set on a fish as all the backbone and strength of the rod are in the lower third near the reel seat. This backbone is what drives the hook home. These lighter and ultralight rods are best suited for panfish. When targeting walleye a longer rod (32-inches), such as a St. Croix CCI Dead Eye, allows the walleye to bite the bait feeling minimal resistance from the rod allowing it time to “load up.” This type of setup is perfect for a “deadstick” allowing the walleye to devour the entire bait before feeling the resistance and in turn self hooking itself.

As ice anglers, we know the cold well, but far too often anglers are not dressed appropriately. Wintertime temps are seldom stable and in the upper Midwest, you can count on the wind making it much colder than what your weather app forecasted. Once you’re cold, it’s hard to get warm without leaving the ice for a short period of time. Wet hands make it even worse. Packing a small fishing towel can go a long way as well as extra pair of gloves. You will see many seasoned ice anglers overdressed for good reason. It’s much easier to take off a layer than add a layer that you didn’t bring with you. Striker Ice suits has a huge array of floatation suites, bibs, and jackets that also come with many layering options, making them a go-to for ice suits and accessories.
