Industry News: The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “I Shot Substantial Red,” appeared in the January 1967 concern of Outdoor Life.
  • In a recent development, at 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime.
  • Sources indicate that I might as well quit, I thought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “I Shot Substantial Red,” appeared in the January 1967 concern of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

In a recent development, at 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

Sources indicate that I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Big Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

My thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Major Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

According to recent reports, in front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

It has been revealed that around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

The sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

Industry observers note that though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

Industry observers note that it took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

Industry observers note that the sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

It has been revealed that after what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Major Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

In a recent development, I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

Recent findings suggest that my .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Major Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

In a recent development, this dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

By the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

Looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

Three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

In a recent development, I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

In 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

It has been revealed that after I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my big six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

We met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

On one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

According to recent reports, about 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

It has been revealed that then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Substantial Red.

I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

In a recent development, the huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

Recent findings suggest that I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

Industry observers note that we must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”.

“That’s Significant Red,” he said. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of company if you figure on hunting that buck.”.

Sources indicate that as it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

Industry observers note that all of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources unveiled that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Massive Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

Sources indicate that A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Big Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

Dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy said as he braked the car.

Recent findings suggest that “No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

It has been revealed that “That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he remarked. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”.

In a recent development, “That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”.

It has been revealed that “That’s the place,” Ross remarked. “I’d forget your other plans and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”.

Industry observers note that that’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the significant sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Industry observers note that about 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

According to recent reports, “I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he said. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a significant one!”.

It has been revealed that rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

Rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Significant Red.

According to recent reports, I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Massive Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

According to recent reports, my change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

Recent findings suggest that at the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

In a recent development, suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

According to recent reports, he might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

According to recent reports, the range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

In a recent development, big Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

It has been revealed that I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

Recent findings suggest that four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Big Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

In a recent development, A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

Industry observers note that two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a upcoming world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Massive Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

In a recent development, the inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Big Red’s.

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

Lessons I Learned from Deer Hunting with My Kids

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a span of maybe a dozen years, from when my twin boys were 11 until their kid sister went to college, we together killed an average of six deer a year, mainly bucks but a few antlerless whitetails and mule deer when we needed the meat.

Industry observers note that that’s a lot of early mornings in northeastern Montana, a lot of cold feet and wintry weather, and a lot of cutting and wrapping and sausage grinding. The body count is a poor measure of our experiences together, though, as it doesn’t tally countless blown stalks, missed shots, and those curiously memorable days when we didn’t see anything worth shooting but we found arrowheads and bison skulls and watched waves of sandhill cranes migrate south. Or those days we talked about fickle friends, where grandparents go when they die, and the notion of self-reliance.

What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.

My kids are freshly gone from the home place. My boys have grown-up jobs in cities on opposite coasts. My daughter is in her first year of graduate school in California.

In the years they’ve been away, I’ve realized how little I care about all the deer-season conversations that used to pique my interest: best days of the rut, the perfect deer caliber, various hacks to unlock locked-up bucks. Instead, I now nourish myself during deer season with a handful of rich lessons accumulated with my kids. If you can excuse the musings of an empty-nest father, here are some of our experiences that still speak to me, years later.

In a recent development, for a confirmed skeptic, I’ll allow the presence of mystery in many parts of my life. How else can I explain the fact that my wife of 29 years still finds me funny or that the nib of a lead pencil that Eric Thompson stabbed me with back in third grade is still in the roll-over flab of my waistline?

According to recent reports, here’s more evidence of mystery. On my son Ellis’s very first deer hunt, after we decided a mule deer doe would be a great way to begin a long hunting career, we were set up on a cottonwood limb that offered a solid rest for Ellis’s .243. Our little stand overlooked a corner of an alfalfa field that spilled into sagebrush and then into a prairie stream that’s a favorite bedding area for mule deer.

It has been revealed that on cue, the deer started filing toward the alfalfa field. Ellis had practiced dry-firing and panning his gun on the branch. Now he was loaded and ready, and, as if scripted, a yearling mule deer walked into view, not 80 yards away, just on the other side of an old barbed-wire fence. Strangely calm as the deer turned broadside to contemplate mule-deery things, Ellis sent one.

Watching from over his shoulder, I expected the deer to crumple, or maybe take the hit and lurch. But the deer just stood there looking at us, and I saw no dust or other evidence of the shot. Now El was rattled.

Recent findings suggest that “What do I do?” he hissed over his shoulder. “Rack another one,” I whispered back. But the deer had had enough and was gone.

Industry observers note that I was sure El had pulled the shot. After all, hadn’t I missed the first couple deer I had shot at when I was his age? It’s natural to be twitchy when confronted for the first time with the reality of taking an animal’s life. Only Ellis insisted that he had been calm and steady.

According to recent reports, “Let’s go make sure you didn’t cut hair or draw any blood,” I stated. Ellis cleared his chamber and we walked toward the first fence, crossed it, and inspected the spot where the deer had been standing when El shot. No blood. No hair. No evidence of a hit. We walked back to our hide, and that’s when I saw it, a freshly clipped vertical cross wire in the first fence.

It has been revealed that ellis went back to the cottonwood limb, and used a straight stick to line up where his rifle had pointed at the deer. It was perfectly aligned with the fence. His .243-caliber bullet had cut the .150-inch-diameter wire, deflecting his shot and saving that deer.

On the way back to the house, Ellis seemed to metabolize the events that had just unfolded.

“Maybe there’s a reason I missed,” he mused. “Maybe it wasn’t time. Maybe I’ll find that deer later.”.

Industry observers note that I have no way of knowing if any of the future mule deer Ellis killed descended from that lucky yearling, but in the years since, I’ve hit limbs instead of vitals, had bullets deflect off unseen sagebrush, and once had an eagle spook a dandy buck just as I was about to shoot. It’s the hidden hand of happenstance. Some people call it fate. Some call it luck. Whenever it happens to me, it conjures Ellis and the pigtailed wire that spoiled his first sure-thing hunt.

It has been revealed that ellis’s twin brother, Merlin, is the most coachable kid I’ve known, and I say that as a longtime coach of track and cross-country runners, some of whom are not related to me. Merlin listens well, follows directions, and is committed to a shared outcome.

So it baffled me just a little when, after graduating from Montana’s Hunter Education course and living under my tutelage about the proper place to shoot a deer, he proceeded to take a neck shot on his first deer.

The doe went about 3 feet, straight down. Lucky, I told him. A few inches high or low and you miss. A couple inches right, you blow the jaw off and the deer dies a horrible death, ultimately of starvation. But Merlin correctly noted that a proper neck shot saves a lot of meat.

According to recent reports, his next couple deer also fell to neck shots. Every time, I reminded him of the risks of the shot, and about the forgiveness of the “boiler room” behind the front shoulder that takes out both lungs and maybe the top of the heart.

It has been revealed that merlin’s rifle was a Ruger No. 1 single-shot chambered in .243. It’s not the most accurate rifle in my collection, but Merlin shot it well, and over the years I came to learn that he had supreme confidence in that gun, and in his one-and-done shot. It’s not my nature to stay quiet — especially when I’m right — but I piped down, and was quietly overjoyed to skin and butcher deer that had four intact quarters and no internal injuries.

I came to realize that Merlin knew something I didn’t. He knew precisely where he was sending that bullet, because he wouldn’t take a shot outside the proficiency zone of his gun and his abilities. When a shot exceeded that distance, he aimed for the boiler room. I came to recognize that his quiet belief in his own abilities has given Merlin opportunities that might never come to a blustery self-promoter.

It was hard to know if hunting would take hold of Iris after her first year. She was a little tentative, in part because we hired a videographer to document her experiences – you can watch it here. Who subjects an 11-year-old girl to that indignity? But despite her initial reluctance, Iris became the most dedicated and determined hunter of my three kids. And, especially after my boys went on to college, hunting was something we shared and nurtured.

Industry observers note that but Iris was burdened by an unseen weight that I’ve observed in other hunters, especially in women and girls. She was so cautious about making a perfect shot that she sometimes allowed otherwise pretty good opportunities to dissolve and then evaporate as she waited for the platonic textbook broadside.

I’ve learned from a lifetime in the field and elsewhere that perfection sometimes isn’t clear in the moment. It can be vanishingly quick to come and go, so quick that many of us scarcely notice it. That quartering-away shot that exposes the vitals of a buck is nearly as good as a broadside shot, I might argue, but Iris was deaf to my suggestions that she relax her standards in this single situation.

It has been revealed that happily, as she’s grown older, Iris has relaxed her expectations while maintaining her high standards. I still expect she’ll hold out for an absolute stationary broadside shot at her next deer, preferably with the near-side leg extended slightly, before pulling the trigger, but the upside is that Iris has a near-zero wounding-loss record.

As an imperfect human, who am I to encourage less of anyone, especially my one and only daughter? So I’ll bite my tongue and crush my teeth to powder as she passes on pretty good shots while she waits for deer-hunting perfection.

Industry observers note that I recognize too late that I was a tyrannical hunting mentor to my kids. If they failed to do things my way, I became a hard-hearted scold. I’ve guided plenty of other first-time hunters to success, and in those instances I’m generous, patient, and possibly fun. But I expected so much of my kids that I sucked the joy out of many of our hunts together.

In a recent development, ellis was the first to go. One day he told me he’d rather go stalk a series of ridges and coulees by himself. That first experience in going it alone became the norm. Later that season, I headed out with the other kids to hunt elk in the Missouri Breaks, but Ellis noted he’d stay back on the ranch and try to scratch out a deer.

In a recent development, we returned after dark to find the house dark and no sign of Ellis. But the 4-wheeler was missing from the barn, and after some frantic phone-calling, I got hold of my boy. He had shot a deer, he said, way across the ranch, and his friend Brett had come to help, but now they were lost in the dark. I got a fix on their location and drove my own 4-wheeler to the spot. The headlights illuminated a crime scene. Blood covered nearly an acre of sagebrush, and then Ellis came into view. Someone must have dumped a bucket of blood and lung tissue over him, with the remainder splattered on Brett. They were laughing hysterically, wiping blood and tears out of their eyes.

It has been revealed that it was the worst field dressing I’ve ever seen, but nobody cared. Ellis had done it. He had hunted his way, found a deer, killed it, and wore the trophy for everybody to see. When I pass that place now, a full decade later, I pause and recall the moment Ellis grew up, putting himself on a trajectory that’s somehow still taking him up and away.

Iris was in her first years of hunting when Chronic Wasting Disease was first detected in our county. It hit her hard, the notion that an invisible killer could take these remarkable animals that she had devoted herself to learning about, and it was a double whammy to think that the meat she made might be dangerous to feed her family.

Recent findings suggest that so in the first years of CWD monitoring, Iris insisted that we test every deer we shot. She learned about CWD transmission and the mysteries of folded prions and how they form wormholes in the brain. She learned how to extract lymph nodes from our deer. When we hunted, she watched deer for signs of sickness. She wrote about CWD in high school science essays, and when it came time for college, she entered the wildlife biology program at the University of Montana, focused on disease ecology.

Read Next, by the Same Author: An Old-School Western Mule Deer Hunt in Memory of Two Midwestern Dads.

Industry observers note that now in graduate school, she’s expanded her gaze to include other wildlife diseases that have the potential to infect humans. She’s learning how to develop vaccines and studying the importance of healthy ecosystems as the first defense against disease.

And she can’t wait to return next week to hunt with me, to rekindle the spark of discovery that began when she was a little girl behind binoculars, watching deer and deciding if they looked delicious enough to take home.

The market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache. That is especially true in light-tackle and inshore fishing, easily the most popular market for spinning reel manufacturers. At first glance, many reels in the 2500-size class, the standard size for this category, look identical. Appearances can be deceiving, though, and knowing how and where you plan to use a reel matters more in this class than in most others.

After all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price? It turns out there are plenty of reasons, and Shimano makes the case for most of them with its updated Sustain FK series.

The Sustain FK gets its strength and light weight from Hagane metal body technology, a process of cold-forging rigid metals such as aluminum and magnesium. As part of Shimano’s MagnumLite series, the metal frame is also paired with an ultralight CI4+ carbon rotor. The result is a reel that feels solid and strong where it should, while staying smooth and light in use.

It has been revealed that the Sustain FK uses DuraCross, a relatively upcoming drag system from Shimano. The idea is that precisely layered materials give the reel a smoother, longer-lasting drag than older materials such as felt. Inside, the reel uses S A-RB bearings, which are shielded and rust-resistant to keep debris out. That adds a layer of protection against sand and salt, which helps keep the reel working in the saltwater conditions it was built for. Shimano also uses what it calls X-Protect, essentially a labyrinth of barriers that makes it far more difficult for salt water or grit to reach the interior of the reel.

No reel is invincible to the hazards of extended saltwater use, but the Sustain FK has a number of features that make it well suited to the task. Corrosion-resistant materials in the frame and gearing, S A-RB sealed bearings and Shimano’s X-Protect design give this reel several strong defenses against the wear and tear of frequent saltwater exposure. Shimano also pairs the DuraCross drag with its Rigid Support Drag to give this small reel a surprisingly strong backbone. The DuraCross drag in particular is a serious upgrade from the standard felt or carbon washers of previous models.

Shimano offers a one-year service warranty on its reels, including the Sustain FK. After that year, you can still send the reel in for service, and Shimano will usually inspect it and tell you the cost before doing the work. Experiences vary, but I’ve sent reels to Shimano countless times over the years and have found its warranty and service system easy to deal with and accommodating.

Sources indicate that shimano touts the Sustain FK as a crossover reel for fresh water and inshore salt water, with a combination of light finesse and rigid durability suited to both. With that in mind, I fished it in a wide range of environments over the course of a year, from bass fishing on large lakes and rivers with a variety of techniques to inshore saltwater fishing that ranged from shallow flats to deep near-shore jigging. The goal was to see whether it could stand up to the all-purpose abuse dished out by hardcore anglers nationwide while still delivering the refinement and finesse expected of a top-end spinning reel in the age of forward-facing sonar. Fishing from both boats and kayaks, I caught largemouth and smallmouth bass, redfish, striped bass and speckled trout.

Corrosion will always be the No. 1 concern when using any reel in salt water, especially one as small and lightweight as the Sustain FK 2500. To get a proper idea of how this reel holds up, I spent the better part of a year fishing with it from my kayak in places like Chesapeake Bay and Laguna Madre in Texas.

A kayak is a great place to test how a reel holds up to the salt because the reel gets so much more direct exposure. Spray tends to reach reels sitting in kayak rod holders, and splashing water is much closer to your gear during high-intensity moments like fighting fish or navigating heavy current. Then there are the times anglers (myself included) accidentally submerge their gear when they aren’t paying attention.

According to recent reports, so, how did the Sustain FK hold up? Remarkably well, I’m pleased to say. After roughly eight months of consistent, heavy saltwater use, the reel is still about as smooth as the day I opened it. It needs some basic maintenance, such as a freshwater rinse and a coat of reel oil now and then, but overall, I’m very impressed.

Recent findings suggest that smoothness matters, but a viable saltwater spinning reel needs a lot more than that. Saltwater game fish are bigger, stronger and live in harsher environments than most freshwater species, and a light spinning reel needs the backbone to stand up to that kind of abuse regularly without losing function. This is where the Sustain FK impressed me most. I intentionally used it in situations where the odds of hooking fish well outside its class were high, and I was able to fight and land everything from bull redfish to large striped bass around heavy cover without the reel bending or warping. The drag may be the reel’s best feature. It stayed smooth and clean during long runs that would have fried the drag on many reels in its class. The Rigid Support system was just as impressive. A reel this light will typically flex under that much strain, but the Sustain FK stayed rigid and smooth.

Ultimately, the Sustain FK passed every saltwater test with flying colors.

It has been revealed that being able to land saltwater fish well outside its intended class is great, but a high-end spinning reel should perform best at what it is intended for. That means no hiccups with anti-reverse or drag slippage, and handling line twist and line lay well. Today, it also means having the fine-tuning required for the extremely finesse-oriented game of fishing with forward-facing sonar. Love it or hate it, forward-facing sonar has become a standard part of professional angling, especially in the bass world.

Sources indicate that with all that in mind, I used the Sustain FK for a wide range of freshwater applications. It performed well in traditional settings like fishing light jigs for river smallmouth bass and crappie, but that’s admittedly not a demanding test. Where this reel really shone was targeting bass on large, deep lakes where finesse and control at depth were key. Fishing with and without forward-facing sonar, I was impressed with the amount of control I could keep on the lure. From jerkbaits to small soft plastics, it never faltered with line management or fine-tuned movements.

The anti-twist fin that Shimano builds into the line roller on many of its high-end reels may sound like a gimmick, but trust me, it makes a big difference. There’s not much worse than light braid twisting while you try to make long casts or present a bait at depth. It can cause wind knots and a host of other issues. Throughout testing, the line on this reel never kinked, twisted or laid poorly on the spool.

Sources indicate that finally, while the smooth, strong drag is great in salt water, the ability to fine-tune it is even more impressive for finesse fishing in fresh water. Getting a solid hook set in deep water on leader as light as 6-pound test can be critical for serious anglers, and that requires a drag that doesn’t slip or freeze up. The Sustain FK drag can be adjusted to the most minute settings, allowing for just the right resistance when setting the hook or playing fish on light line.

I can’t remember using a reel that was as much at home fishing ultralight for crappie and perch as it was fishing a marsh for drag-ripping bull redfish and striped bass. I may be in the minority, but I love having a lightweight 2500-size spinning reel that pulls double duty as both my favorite freshwater finesse setup and my favorite inshore spinning rig. The crossover ability of the Sustain FK is fantastic. It’s not just a good freshwater reel that’s decent in the salt, or a saltwater reel that’s light enough to use in fresh water. It’s at the top of its game in both.

The Sustain FK is an exceptional reel, so finding areas for improvement is difficult. The most obvious is the price. The engineering and performance can justify it, but there’s no denying that nearly $400 for a light spinning reel is steep for the average angler. There are plenty of equally light and smooth spinning reels on the market for far less. Those reels may not match the Sustain FK’s quality and durability across the board, but those features probably don’t matter as much to many freshwater or casual inshore anglers.

If you’re looking for a light-tackle spinning reel that’s durable and strong while still being incredibly smooth and light, the Sustain FK is the ideal choice. It’s comfortable to fish in both fresh and salt water, with the refinement needed for the most finesse-oriented applications.

Recent findings suggest that this review focused on the 2500, but the Sustain FK presently comes in sizes from 2500 through 5000. The limited size range is a downside, but given that this reel is designed for such a specific level of performance, it makes sense to offer it only in sizes that don’t compromise that.

Read Next: The Best Fishing Kayaks.

Although the price tag isn’t cheap, this reel is the complete package for serious anglers who want professional-grade performance from their gear. Tournament bass anglers and hardcore inshore anglers alike will appreciate the refinement the Sustain FK delivers over similar-size, budget-friendly options.

Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate aims to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.
  • The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
  • BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Senate aims to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

Industry observers note that that means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

In a recent development, but sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

“I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life. “Because when I say climate change is an existential threat, I mean it. And I will not let an opportunity to do something about it pass by.”.

Conservationists like Ingrid Lyons, executive director of Save the Boundary Waters, understand the need for stability around permitting development. The whiplash between issuing and revoking permits for public land development projects every time an administration changes has likely hurt the U.S.’s ability to move forward with important energy projects, including in renewables like wind and solar.

But she fears this bill could instead cement the creation of controversial projects like a copper-sulfide mine at the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or a copper-molybdenum-gold mine in the salmon-rich waters of Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Permits for projects like these have been denied, among other issues, because of environmental risk. If permits are reissued in similar scenarios, legislation like BAAJA could prevent future administrations from stopping development in places that truly need protection.

Sources indicate that “What about landscape certainty?” Lyons indicates. “We’re overlooking in some ways the impact to communities that are relying on protection and not just projects.”.

The conservation community has become increasingly vocal in its opposition to the bill since Heinrich and Lee partnered with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), to introduce the legislation in late September. Lee has a clear track record of supporting public land sales and undermining existing public-lands conservation, including 2025’s attempt to include federal land sales in the One Massive Beautiful Bill.

A lengthy version of BAAJA is before the Senate as of Tuesday. The current bill includes a variety of red flags for hunters, anglers, tribes, endangered-species advocates, and other conservationists.

Some of the main points include:.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership acknowledged the need for permit reform but remarked in a statement that “progress should not come at the expense of the conservation safeguards and public review that give hunters and anglers a voice in how our lands and waters are managed.”.

For Lyons, it comes down to the potential unintended consequences of sweeping legislation like BAAJA.

“We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”.

Many in the conservation community were surprised by the bill’s sponsors, given Heinrich’s history as a sportsman and conservationist who regularly defends public lands and sensitive places, and Lee’s general position as a proponent of development and public-lands sell-off.

According to recent reports, but in Heinrich’s statement to Outdoor Life, he emphasizes the impact of climate change on our planet, including the places where people hunt, hike, bike and camp. Independent modeling, he said, predicts the bill will lead to a 20 percent reduction in power sector emissions, or the “equivalent to taking 39 coal plants offline for 10 years.”.

Sources indicate that “You cannot protect a trout stream without paying attention to the warming temperatures and declining flows that threaten it,” he wrote. “You cannot protect wildlife habitat while ignoring the impacts of increasingly severe drought and wildfire. We need to reduce emissions, and that means getting more clean energy onto the grid.”.

In an Oct. 30 op-ed in the Albuquerque Journal, Heinrich explained how Upcoming Mexico’s SunZia Wind and Transmission project took 17 years to permit and build.

He also pushed back on what he called misinformation about the bill, stating he doesn’t believe data centers should be on public land. The bill also requires large scale data center operators to pay the full cost of electricity consumed by the facility.

In a recent development, the Izaak Walton League’s conservation director, Kate Miller, thinks each of the bill’s sponsors are acting in good faith and trying to do what is right for their constituents. Many projects, including those aimed at restoring forests and wildlife habitat, have been held up by permitting delays. Something like BAAJA could move those forward.

But Miller would have liked to see these complications tackled individually instead of in a massive bill. And while she hopes that, if the bill passes, the administration will respect existing laws, the past two years has brought an onslaught of changes to most of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

“We want to make sure what comes out is not something that sacrifices those core protections that allow us to have healthy waters and habitats,” Miller notes. “That we don’t sacrifice one for the other.”.

In a recent development, while the Senate is fast tracking the bill before the next Congress begins in January, it must move through the Senate and the House, and any changes be agreed upon by both chambers before the bill would land on President Trump’s desk. Meanwhile, both industry and conservation groups say they’re working to lobby lawmakers for changes and amendments. As a result, several conservation organizations declined to comment for this story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.

On Nov. 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.

His guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets. The dismissed charges include two for poaching, trespass, motorized aid and failure to retrieve game. Both of the killed animals were bull elk, one antlerless and the other a 6×6 which was on private property. Harshbarger was accompanied by another man, Eric Murphy, at the time.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

In a recent development, “Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull,” according to investigation documents obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property in violation of Idaho Code.”.

Harshbarger had already filled his elk tag the weekend before the two bulls were shot. His hometown, Ashton, is in the same county where the violations took place. That same county, Fremont, borders Yellowstone National Park and is in the region Harshbarger represents on the state’s seven-person commission. That commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists.

Each member of the commission, most often a resident hunter and/or fisherman, is appointed by the governor for a term of four years with a two-term maximum. The commission meets at least four times a year. Harshbarger hasn’t attended those meetings since his case opened after a tip received through the department’s Citizens Against Poaching in December. He hasn’t resigned and the Governor hasn’t dismissed him, but his profile has been removed from the commission’s website.

According to recent reports, “The Governor’s office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Gov. Brad Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan told the Sun. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”.

Industry observers note that harshbarger was appointed to the commission in 2024. His sentencing for illegal activities in 2025 is scheduled for Dec. 9. With the upcoming plea deal and the number of charges reduced, the fine is expected to be $500 plus a one-year loss of hunting privileges.

For winter snowshoeing on hiking trails and in the backcountry, you want a durable snowshoe with aggressive crampons for traction and a secure binding system that locks your boots to the snowshoes. If you want to get off the grid and snowshoe through backcountry terrain, here are our 10 recommended snowshoes. For more information, see our buying advice below.

It has been revealed that winter hiking snowshoes serve two key functions: they provide traction on icy trails and when climbing steep terrain, and they provide flotation over snow, so you don’t sink or posthole, which can be quite exhausting. While all the winter hiking snowshoes listed above meet both requirements, some excel in traction, like the MSR Lightning Ascents, MSR Evo Ascents, and Tubbs Flex VRTs, while others emphasize flotation, like the Tubbs Mountaineers.

As a rule of thumb, teardrop-shaped snowshoes with synthetic, riveted decks tend to emphasize flotation, while rectangular snowshoes focus more on traction. If you’ll be climbing ice-covered mountains mostly, you’ll probably want a snowshoe that emphasizes traction; snowshoes that focus on flotation are better for areas where deep, powdery snow is the norm.

If you’re trying to choose between different snowshoes, there are four key properties that should guide your decision-making:.

Most winter hikers carry multiple traction devices and switch between them during the day. If you’re hiking a packed trail, you might start in bare boots, relying on your boot treads for traction because less weight on your feet means you’ll fatigue more slowly. If you hit slick or icy terrain, you might switch to microspikes, then snowshoes if you encounter fresh, uncompacted snow or slush.

Industry observers note that to have these traction aids when you need them, you need to carry them. Microspikes are pretty easy to pack, but snowshoes aren’t because they’re substantial and bulky. Their bulk comes from their length, width, and thickness, which depends largely on the binding style they use. Lay-flat bindings, like the simple straps on the MSR Lightning Ascent and the MSR Evo Ascent, make snowshoes easy to attach and carry in a backpack, while snowshoes with Boa binding systems tend to be the bulkiest and hardest to pack.

Industry observers note that weight is also a key factor when choosing a snowshoe. Most snowshoes weigh four to five pounds, and they’re probably going to be the heaviest thing in your backpack, after water. That weight adds up over the course of a day, whether it’s in your backpack or on your feet.

We’ve already considered the packability of snowshoe bindings, but you should also consider comfort, security, ease of use while wearing gloves, whether the binding can freeze and become inoperative, and how easy it is to repair if it breaks. For example, some people worry that Boa closure systems can freeze if they get wet and stop working until they thaw. It’s a valid concern. One advantage, however, is that they are easy to use while wearing gloves and provide a secure grip that’s unlikely to come undone once set. Contrast that to the flat straps used on MSR snowshoes. They’ll never freeze up, they’re easy to replace if torn or lost, but they can be hard to attach when wearing gloves, and they tend to pop open once or twice during a hike.

According to recent reports, snowshoes come in a wide variety of sizes. These are determined by the total weight you want to carry (body weight + pack weight) and the flotation you need. Men’s sizes are usually larger than women’s because men are taller and heavier, while women’s snowshoes tend to be narrower because their gait is narrower.

If you’re buying a more traction-oriented snowshoe, you can sometimes drop a size below the manufacturer’s recommendation, especially if you’re hiking in an area that doesn’t get much snow or on trails that other hikers have already broken out. Sizing is directly correlated to gear weight and this is a tactic you can use to lighten your load. If flotation is a priority, you can buy tails, add-on snowshoe extensions that make them longer and increase their surface area. This is another way to cut down on the weight of a snowshoe because you can bring your tails when you need more flotation, but carry a lighter-weight snowshoe in less challenging conditions.

#56185. Latest Update: Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Big Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Big Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies.
  • Sources indicate that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks.
  • Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies. He’s honed these strategies through decades of hard hunting and consulting on his clients’ properties. He’s also tested them on his own 170-acre property in the bluff country of southern Minnesota (you can follow him on his YouTube channel, Whitetail Habitat Solutions).

Sources indicate that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks. In the video above, Sturgis runs through his five favorite setups and explains how he hunts them. Some of these setups take an immense amount of work and expense to develop. Others require minimal habitat work but a deep understanding of deer behavior.

Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.

Everyone talks about “buck bedding areas” but many hunters have only a vague understanding of them. The important point, Sturgis says, is that bucks do not like to bed near a lot of commotion, and that includes commotion from other deer. For example, does will often bed near major food sources. It’s convenient for them to get up from their bed and stroll right into a large food plot or ag field.

Mature bucks don’t like to bed around a mass of other deer. So buck beds will be found farther away from main food sources — even if there is prime bedding habitat right by those food sources. So just because you’re seeing a lot of does and young bucks in an area doesn’t mean it’s a good spot for mature bucks. In fact, it could mean the opposite.

By crossing off areas where mature bucks won’t bed — again, areas with high pressure and activity — you can narrow down where they will bed. Sturgis isn’t afraid to hunt near buck bedding areas, but he does so sparingly. And when he does, he often takes his target buck.

When you see deer consistently coming to a big food plot or agricultural field during daylight hours, it’s tempting to just hunt that major food source. Sturgis will hunt the big “holding plot” on his property, but only when he’s able to do so without spooking deer. He’s got a Redneck blind at the edge of the plot, which has an access route that is completely blocked by screening cover. He can get into and out of the blind with deer in the field — and never spook them. But that setup means he’s only able to hunt the big holding plot during gun season, even if there are target bucks hitting it during bow season.

In a recent development, sturgis considers the holding plot the cornerstone of his entire property. So long as deer feel safe feeding there, he’s in the game. Even if he happens to bump a buck out of its bedding area, that deer is likely to switch bedding areas but still come to the holding plot to feed. This means that Sturgis can keep hunting that buck.

Sources indicate that on the flipside, if he blows out the holding plot, it throws off deer behavior for the entire property, and that could be detrimental to his entire season. In some ways, he treats the holding plot like a sanctuary.

Industry observers note that sturgis has a ton of videos about how to set up and hunt waterholes. He creates his waterhole setups in the woods in traditional rut funnels. These waterholes give deer a reason to come within bow range and to stop there. Sturgis and his wife, Jen, have some of their best substantial-buck hunts over waterholes.

In a recent development, these setups are relatively easy to implement, assuming you can get some kind of water tank into the woods where you hunt. They’re great places for all-day sits during the heart of the rut.

In a recent development, we all love to be in the woods before sunrise and to hear the telltale sound of a buck marching into range just after shooting light. But in some cases it’s impossible to hunt a spot first thing in the morning without spooking deer. These are often areas near field edges — deer are still in the fields feeding in the dark.

It has been revealed that in these scenarios Sturgis will simply enter the stand an hour or so after daylight when deer have left the field. This allows him to slip in undetected and have several hours of quality hunting before leaving again in the evening. These are usually high-probability sits during the rut.

The main principle that Sturgis’ hunting strategy revolves around is to not overpressure mature deer. He wants big bucks to do their thing: rut, establish their dominance, and move around the habitat, during daylight hours. He lets his Tactacam trail cameras do the monitoring, and he picks his sits carefully. Of course we all love being in the woods and Sturgis does too. So he has stands that are very low impact for those times when he or someone in his family just wants to hunt — and you never know, a mature buck could stroll by any time.

But his approach is much more surgical when really targeting a specific deer.

One of the many things I learned from Sturgis is that all of the knowledge (and much more) outlined above has been built into the Habitat IQ app. This app allows the user to draw in habitat features (like food sources, water, timber, and roads) into their own property. The program then uses a powerful algorithm, built off of Sturgis’ knowledge, to make habitat improvement suggestions and predict deer movement.

For example, if you don’t have any useful water sources on your property, the app will suggest adding some waterholes, and give you an idea about the best areas to place them.

Related: Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to Jeff Sturgis.

The app is basically a digital version of Sturgis’ habitat/hunting consulting business. The more data you add into it, the better information you get back. I think this will be an incredibly powerful tool for anyone who is looking to implement the concepts that Sturgis has proven out over the course of 20-plus years of consulting on deer properties.
