📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that southeastern Ohio is known for its heavily wooded rolling hills and the major bucks that live there. Margaret Fuller of Fresh Plymouth has hunted a small piece of private land there for years, and it’s where she was hunting this past weekend. In particular, she was looking for a giant 200-class buck she’d come to think of as “the Monarch.”.

The substantial deer started showing up on trail camera about a month ago, although only at night. He was hitting scrapes near one of Fuller’s favorite ladder stands, and that’s where she hunted on Friday.

“It was bitter cold that day, but I hunted from the morning until noon,” Fuller tells Outdoor Life. “I went inside to get warm for a while, then went back out that afternoon and hunted until dark.”.

It has been revealed that that day she spotted a smaller buck about 50 yards from her stand. The deer was working along a trail toward her, but seemed to sense something was wrong and slipped away.

Fuller returned to that same stand the next day — her birthday — anyway. It’s the same spot she killed a 178-inch buck in 2022 during the firearms season.

“I didn’t get on stand until about noon,” says Fuller, a financial program manager for the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, “because I was so cold from the previous day’s hunt.”.

Industry observers note that about 3 p.m. she heard an ATV roaring on the neighbor’s property and she thought her hunt that afternoon was over.

“But a few minutes later I heard something in the woods, and then I caught a little movement,” says Fuller. “I stood up, grabbed my crossbow, and saw it was Monarch.”.

He was at 50 yards and coming to a scrape along the same trail the little buck had walked the day before.

It has been revealed that “I was worried the Monarch would spook, too, like the smaller buck did. I knew I had to shoot soon before he caught my wind.”.

The buck began stopped to rub his rack on a tree, then started walking closer to Fuller.

It has been revealed that “I knew I had to stop him before he got to the place where he could smell me, so I grunted,” indicates Fuller. “He stopped when I grunted, and I shot him at 30 yards.”.

It has been revealed that instead of running, the buck dropped right there. Her shot had struck the spine, and the deer didn’t get up.

Fuller called her sons and husband, then climbed down from her ladder stand.

It has been revealed that “I was on cloud nine,” she claims. “I’ve been hunting deer since I was 14 with my dad, and I’d have given anything for him to have been with me and see this buck … And it was on my birthday, too!”.

The family helped Fuller snap photos and field-dress the massive nontypical, which had 20 points. Then they butchered the deer at home.

The whitetail, which Fuller estimates is 5½ years old, was scored at 213 inches by Buckmasters measurer Toby Hughes.

“I’m over the moon,” claims Fuller, who credits her success, in part, to “sticking with hunting even in the coldest weather.”.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

She also adds that practicing meticulous scent control with her clothing and using a cover scent probably didn’t hurt, either.

Sources indicate that “But the best thing is the joy of having my sons and husband involved in hunting. Everyone helped me and that family camaraderie is really special.”.

According to recent reports, it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle. But choosing one, for a first-time buyer, can be intimidating. There are thousands of options on the market and narrowing it down to the best can for your hunting rifle isn’t easy if you don’t know what to look for. So many new suppressors are hitting the market that what was a top-of-the-line can a couple years ago is just average today.

I’ve been shooting every new suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.

This is one of the best hunting rifle suppressors I have ever used. Like many others that are leading the pack, it’s 3D printed from titanium, making it both strong and economical. It measures 5 inches long and weighs just 5.75 ounces. Despite its lightweight profile, it’s very quiet. In fact, it’s substantially quieter than several other popular suppressors — something I noted on a recent antelope hunt.

This is one of my top picks because it’s simple, rugged, quiet, and you’ll hardly notice it on your muzzle. It is direct thread only and, because threads are cut into the suppressor itself, they cannot be changed like a HUB-compatible suppressor. For a hunting suppressor, that’s a feature, not a bug. At $900, this is a really good value. Many top-level hunting suppressors will cost you $1,000 or more.

Sources indicate that in the year since its introduction, Airlock has released 30-cal and 7mm versions of the Zero Gravity, as well as a 3.7-ounce Zero Gravity Nano, which is designed for bolt-action centerfire .22 cals like the 22 ARC, 22 Creed, and .22-250 Rem. It’s slightly larger than a rimfire suppressor, but satisfyingly quiet.

The Nomad Ti XC is another excellent option for a hunting suppressor. Its 3D printed design allows for modern baffles and reduces weak spots. The front and rear of the can are threaded and it is compatible with HUB rear mounts. I prefer using a Silencerco Ti direct thread adapter on the rear, and the standard .308 front cap. Other companies like Salmon River Solutions are making accessories like a directional brake that threads into the front cap to further reduce recoil and tame down cartridges like the .300 PRC. As pictured, the suppressor weighs less than 10 ounces and works wonderfully for anything 30-caliber and under. A nice feature is the inclusion of deep tool notches which makes removing the HUB mounts easy without worry of damaging the suppressor.

Sources indicate that another great option, if you want a shorter overall length for your rifle, is the Nomad TiOTB, which has a chamber that extends back over the barrel. This suppressor has the same interchangeable endcaps, but works exclusively with a thread-over-brake mount.

I’ve been shooting the TiTrex 300 Ti for several months now, and this is one of the best options for a general-purpose hunting suppressor out there. After all that shooting, it still only weighs 9.5 ounces, and it offers great mounting and front-cap modularity.

In a recent development, A couple years ago, the Silencerco Scythe Ti was one of few .30-cal silencers that light, but it’s been plagued by weld failure issues. The TiTrex 300 Ti is also made of titanium, is slightly lighter, and uses HUB mounts at the rear and an open-source front cap that works with the Silencerco Bravo front mounts. You can use a normal endcap or the short endcap brake, which helps reduce recoil, and both have great spanner wrench notches. It’s also compatible with some aftermarket Endcap brakes like the Salmon River Solutions Grim, which can help cut recoil even more.

Recent findings suggest that the TiTrex has a 3D-printed body and baffle system that is rugged, durable, and even full-auto rated. This is a great option to use with a front brake as a competition can, but that can also work well on your hunting rifle. It would also be a solid choice as your first suppressor. A unique feature is that the serialized portion of the suppressor is a stainless-steel band at the rear of the can, that can be moved to a different core if you manage to wear the original out or damage it somehow.

There are three big trends in hunting suppressors in 2026, and the Buckskin 30 from Tenet tackles all of them. First, it’s 3D printed. Additive manufacturing has allowed companies to swiftly develop and prototype suppressor models while reducing weak points like welds on thin titanium.

It has been revealed that second, it incorporates a front brake. Suppressors reduce recoil by slowing gases as they exit the muzzle, and incorporating a brake on the front tames them even further. The Buckskin features a built-in brake that is non-adjustable and won’t come loose.

According to recent reports, third, it’s light. It’s printed with titanium and mine weighs 8.5 ounces — making it the lightest .30-cal suppressor I own. I’ve used this suppressor on my 20-inch 300 PRC, several 6.5 Creedmoors, and have been putting a lot of rounds through it on a 16-inch 7mm Backcountry. It does a great job at reducing recoil while adding minimal extra weight.

According to recent reports, if you want more adjustability and increased recoil reduction, the Tenet Limited 30 is another suppressor to look at. These are more expensive, but feature a removable front brake that cuts your rifle movement dramatically. Mine has a two-port brake and, while the first generation of brakes tended to blast your face with gas, the recently-released gen 2 brake has small steps in the curved brake to disrupt that gas impulse. It’s much more pleasant. If spotting your impacts with larger cartridges is important to you, a can like this fits the bill.

In the days of year-long waiting periods, modularity was king for hunting suppressors. While modular cans have their place, a simple dedicated hunting silencer is hard to beat. This fully 3D-printed titanium can from Unknown Munitions weighs about 11 ounces and features a reflex design, meaning the rear portion of the suppressor goes back over the barrel. That reflex expansion chamber allows a shorter portion — about four inches — to stick out in front of your muzzle. This improves balance and gives you a more compact package than the average 8-inch suppressor. The reflex design also creates a noticeably duller sound signature, whereas some produce a very sharp, snappy sound.

It has been revealed that these are available in .30 caliber as well as 6.5mm and 6mm options, and models and fit over 0.75-inch diameter steel barrels and the OGL model fits larger carbon-fiber barrels. This suppressor isn’t modular, so you need to ensure compatibility before you order. Also check out their Reaper suppressor, which I haven’t had the chance to use, but should be another top contender.

I’ve used several of B&T’s Print-X series of titanium 3D-printed suppressors and have been impressed by all of them. Their modular VERS36 Ti model, however, deserves special recognition. To my knowledge, this is the lightest modular 36-caliber suppressor on the market, and it’s way cheaper than similar, more primitive cans were several years ago. If you’re wanting to get a suppressor to start out with, or to use on multiple hunting rifles, this is your jam.

Sources indicate that it’s got 36-caliber baffles and comes with a .360 front cap. The rear is HUB-compatible and B&T makes nice titanium direct-thread adapters. You can get smaller front caps as well. If using on smaller cartridges or you just need a shorter overall package, the front section is removable. This is a flow-through design with spiral baffles that works well on bolt actions and gas-guns alike. It’s ideal for cartridges like the .350 Legend, but will work on anything with a .360-diameter bullet or smaller. I received mine through Silencer Central and it can be delivered to your door.

The StingerWorx Evo Hunter is a lightweight suppressor that’s more affordable than the 3D printed titanium cans, and it’s also much more serviceable. A downside of most printed suppressors is that there isn’t a great way to remove large amounts of carbon buildup from the baffles. Soaking and ultrasonic cleaners help, but a lot of shooters want a suppressor that can be disassembled and manually cleaned.

The Evo Hunter is just over 10 ounces, and it gets there by using multiple materials. It has a titanium blast baffle and chamber to provide a long service life, but uses an aluminum baffle stack downstream of that — where heat and abrasion isn’t as intense. If damaged, that front baffle stack is replaceable. Additionally, the Evo Hunter is compatible with StingerWorx’s front brake if you’re looking for additional recoil reduction. It’s got HUB threads at the rear and the blast chamber is deep enough to work with a variety of over-brake HUB mounts that you might already have. For the light weight, versatility, and serviceability, this can is a great value.

There are lots of suppressors out there and, because many of them are so similar, lots of good ones can get lost in the mix. Because we cover a lot of leading-edge ultralight cans, don’t think that we don’t pay attention to budget options, too. There are bottom-tier suppressors that are very cheap — often made of mostly aluminum — that will work, but can also leave buyers dissatisfied. When it comes to bang for your buck, stainless steel is still one of the best materials for a more affordable can. The first suppressor I ever bought was a large .30-cal stainless can. It was durable and affordable and its weight was the only downside.

Industry observers note that the Banish HNT 30 SS is a great example of a modern great value. It’s compact and, at 13.8 ounces, not excessively heavy. It’s suitable for virtually any hunting rifle .30-caliber and smaller, and similar in size and form to the lightweight Banish Backcountry titanium can. It’s got hub threads at the rear and comes with a direct-thread adapter. If you’re looking to try a suppressor for hunting and want a good-quality can, this is a great place to start.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for maximum suppression of your big-bore cartridges, the Goliath Gen 2 from Liberty Suppressors is an excellent option. This beast of a silencer is 10.25 inches long by 2 inches in diameter and designed specifically for cartridges like the .458 Socom, .450 Bushmaster, and .45/70 Gov’t. While big, this can is relatively light. It’s got twice the volume of suppressors like the Silencerco Hybrid 46, but weighs only about 4 ounces more (22 ounces total). This is a perfect fit for anyone hunting with a short-barreled .458 or .450 Bushmaster, or a trapper-style .45/70.

Sources indicate that the suppressor has a titanium sleeve and titanium baffle stack that’s removable and serviceable so you can shoot cast lead bullets and clean out lead fouling — unlike sealed suppressors. I’ve had a Liberty .22 rimfire can for many years, and this is essentially a much larger version of that. I’ve been shooting it on my .45/70 and it’s working wonderfully on my .338 ARC SBR with subsonic ammo.

One of the best values in lightweight modular suppressors is the BDE from Primary Weapons Systems. I’ve been shooting the 5.56 model for the last several months, and it combines smart manufacturing with durability, value, and the kind of modularity a lot of hunters want. The BDE has hub threads at the rear, a blast chamber segment, and a 3D-printed main baffle segment. Forward of that, it has removable individual threaded baffle segments topped with an end cap.

Sources indicate that this is a sealed suppressor, but baffles are designed to allow gasses to flow better and reduce backpressure, making a great option for both a bolt gun and AR-style semi-auto. Each segment of the can has wrench notches making disassembly easy, and you can customize to the platform you’ll be shooting. This has been living on my .223 practice bolt-action and the irregular surface contours do seem to help break up mirage. The BDE is also available in .30- and .36- caliber models, all with customizable baffle configurations.

Picking through the many different suppressor options can be daunting, and most good suppressors perform similarly. To find one that you’ll be happy with, consider details like construction and weight, but also the level of modularity you desire, or whether you’re just looking for a good value. If one of these isn’t quite what you’re looking for, I hope that seeing these options and features will help you home in on the model that you will be most satisfied with. The suppressor market is constantly evolving, and we will continue to use and test suppressors with the goal of helping you make the most informed decisions possible.

#56165. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Cornfields During Deer Season

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Cornfields During Deer Season

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are two things that my friend Harvey Wilcourt loves more than anything else.
  • According to recent reports, harve and I had scheduled a day of winter fishing for walleyes, and the plan was to meet at a well-known parking area near the lake and then decide upon a particular frozen-over bay that might offer the best results.
  • At first, I shrugged my shoulders, not knowing in which direction he might have headed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are two things that my friend Harvey Wilcourt loves more than anything else. One is ice-fishing, and the other is eating peanuts. It might not sound as though that bears any relation to whitetail deer hunting, but one time it actually helped me to collect a very significant buck.

According to recent reports, harve and I had scheduled a day of winter fishing for walleyes, and the plan was to meet at a well-known parking area near the lake and then decide upon a particular frozen-over bay that might offer the best results. As it happened, however, car trouble delayed my arrival by more than an hour, so naturally, when I finally reached our meeting place, Harve had already headed out onto the ice-shrouded lake.

At first, I shrugged my shoulders, not knowing in which direction he might have headed. Then, I happened to look down at the ground near his parked vehicle, and guess what I spotted? Right, peanut shells! Right then, a wide smile came across my face because I instantly knew that tracking Harve would be easy.

In most places, the trail was relatively thin, but occasionally I’d come to an abandoned hole in the ice where shells littered the entire area. Then, the trail would lead off into the distance to another hole, and then still another. Eventually, I spied my partner in a distant channel, and we spent the remainder of the day fishing together. Without the discarded peanut shells showing the way, I might have never located Harve and might have ended up fishing solo that day.

Recent findings suggest that the irony is that several years later, I duplicated the same type of feat, but this time the trail eventually led me to an eight-point buck. To the best of my knowledge, whitetails don’t maintain any particular fetish for peanuts, but they do love corn. And after filling their paunches in a cornfield, it’s quite common for them to carry off a cob in their mouths and continue eating from it as they travel to a nearby bedding site. Sometimes, they’ll finish with the cob along the way and let it fall to the ground right there. Other times, they’ll carry the cob all the way back to the actual bedding location, perhaps to snack upon later.

In a recent development, in any event, I had been hiking along the edge of a large cornfield near my home in southern Ohio, and in coming upon a threadbare trail exiting from the corn, I had found a partially eaten cob. Recalling my amusing experience with Harvey, I decided to follow the trail, and just inside the leading edge of a nearby beech forest I discovered another cob on the ground, and then still another. All of the cobs were in various stages of deterioration, so I knew that they had been dropped at different times over a period of weeks. Large, fresh deer tracks of uniform size and large droppings provided additional clues, and eventually, more than 300 yards into the timber, I came upon a lone bed. That confirmed I was in a buck’s bailiwick, because had there been tracks of varied sizes and several beds, I could have inferred that the deer were only does.

After resting the area for two days, I snuck back into the spot and quietly fabricated a makeshift blind behind a convenient blowdown overlooking the trail. Later, when there was just enough light to make a shot, a gray shadow materialized in the distance, traveling right along the trail. My arrow caught the eight-pointer at the base of the neck, and after sprinting 50 yards, the buck collapsed in a heap.

According to recent reports, it’s no secret that bucks and corn go together like bacon and eggs, and we have plenty of all of those commodities, especially throughout the Midwestern agricultural belt. In fact, after talking recently with my local extension agent, I learned that in 1986, in the nine major farming states stretching from Ohio to Minnesota, more than 46 million acres of land were planted to corn.

According to recent reports, moreover, acquiring hunting permission in agricultural regions is invariably easier than it is on other privately owned lands because of the extensive damage often inflicted by wild animals. In Wisconsin alone, it was estimated that during 1986, deer destroyed more than $22 million worth of corn, and this cost each farmer an average of $490. Add to this the combined losses of alfalfa, soybeans, truck garden crops and other foods that whitetails regularly dine upon, and it should come as no surprise that though a majority of farmers certainly enjoy seeing deer on their land, they don’t take kindly to whitetail populations reaching such levels that they severely cut into the farmers’ annual incomes.

The exasperating problem that most hunters face is how to effectively hunt those often mammoth and intimidating cornfields.

The first task is to confirm that deer are indeed using the corn, and this is easily ascertained by merely hiking the perimeter of the field and looking for tracks entering and leaving the food plot. Obviously, the best time to do this is either after a rainy period, when the ground is soft, or after several days of light snowfall.

Recent findings suggest that if the region has been experiencing several weeks of dry weather, however, and the terrain is like hardpan, tracks are not easily detected. It is in this case that other types of insight must be applied to the hunting situation. For example, one time I discovered a cornfield where many stalks had been knocked down and countless partially eaten ears were on the ground. Initially, I thought that I had found a mother lode of deer activity, but I was dead wrong.

As I learned later, several raccoons had been at work. The telltale giveaway — pointed out to me by a friend who is a serious naturalist — should have been the fact that the ears were only partially eaten. Raccoons rarely eat an entire ear of corn; instead, they knock down a cornstalk and bite off just the tender tip of the ear, then move on to the next stalk.

If the cornfield borders a climax forest, corn-hungry squirrels may also give the false impression that deer have been at work. But in this situation, the animals climb the stalks, nibble away at the ears, stuff their cheeks and then retreat to their dens, where the scavenged kernels are placed in storage. This leaves the ears still attached to the stalks but gives them a ragtag, moth-eaten appearance.

If deer are working the corn, however, the clues to look for in the absence of tracks are scattered cobs on the ground that have been cleaned of almost every kernel of corn. Also keep on the lookout for droppings.

Once it has been determined that deer are hitting a particular cornfield on a regular basis, the best mode of hunting must be decided upon. And contrary to what you might expect, the best method of hunting is not necessarily the tactic you might like to use most, but rather the one that most appropriately falls in line with the agricultural cropping practices in your region.

In many areas, conventional harvesting methods are engaged in sometime during October or November, when the corn is brown and cured. The picking operation leaves the cornfield in a stubble-like condition, yet there remains on the ground plenty of spillage residue to attract the interest of local deer. Under these conditions, with the previously standing cornstalks no longer present and the concealing cover therefore eliminated, midday hunting is virtually out of the question. The animals will predictably visit the corn only in the early morning hours or at dusk. If hunting pressure is intense in the region, the deer may even be strictly nocturnal in their feeding.

Conversely, in many other regions, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing in the field for as long as possible. With grain-elevator storage costs escalating like never before, and future market prices always uncertain, many farmers nowadays are simply delaying their harvesting either until such time as they have a specific need for the corn for stock feed or until the price increases, which it often does in February or March. Consequently, the hunter now finds that he can effectively hunt the cornfields not only early and late in the day, but also during the midday hours.

Regardless of whether a solo hunter elects to use bowhunting equipment, a rifle, a slug-loaded shotgun, a muzzleloader or a handgun, there are four options to choose from when hunting standing corn: sneak-hunting in and around the corn; sneak-hunting in and around nearby heavy-cover regions; taking a stand designed to intercept the animals coming to the corn; or taking a stand designed to intercept the animals as they leave the corn.

Still again, the right method to use may not necessarily be the hunter’s favorite way to hunt, but it must be geared to existing conditions. The foremost determinant that I rely upon to make my decision is the presence or absence of wind — assuming there is standing corn, of course.

On a windy day, I do not want to be in a tree stand. Wind is the result of downdrafts of cold air meeting warm air. Therefore, no matter which direction the wind is coming from, it will have a tendency to force scents down toward the ground, and this will readily give away a hunter’s location. Compounding the problem is the fact that deer do not like to move on windy days because the wind disallows the effective use of their sense of hearing. Calm days, on the other hand, or those during which the wind is only slightly and gently blowing from one specific direction are ideal for quietly waiting on stand for the deer to walk by.

According to recent reports, just the opposite is the case when hunting in and around the cornfield itself. Now is when a hunter wants the windiest conditions possible. This is because when whitetails bed during the midday hours, they feel most secure and safe by retreating into the heaviest, thickest cover they can find. In many agricultural regions, the terrain surrounding cornfields, such as gullies and forest lands, simply does not offer hiding cover that is as thick as that in the cornfields themselves. Consequently, the whitetails will commonly bed right in the cornfields in these areas.

Now it becomes obvious why the very time to hunt these cornfields is during periods of high winds. It is because under blowing conditions, a cornfield is a very noisy place. The leaves are dry and brittle later in the season, and the loud rustling and crackling noises that they make in the wind cover up so much human error in prowling around that a hunter can quite easily walk right up on deer without them suspecting his presence.

Moreover, a hunter doesn’t have to worry about his scent when hunting in a cornfield. Wind in a cornfield is a tricky thing. It hits the stalks and broad leaves and bounces every which way. As a result, deer in a cornfield may catch a hunter’s scent, but in most cases they will not be able to determine the direction from which it’s coming. As a result, they lock up, or freeze, in position because they know that if they attempt to run, they may blunder right into trouble. And if the hunter then happens to step into the right row of corn, he may have an easy shot at a stationary buck.

Recent findings suggest that in going back to calm days, during which patiently waiting in a tree stand or ground blind is the preferred method of hunting either standing corn or stubble fields, there are two tricks that I use to properly locate my stand. First, it’s necessary to engage in enough scouting to know in advance where trails are located. It must be remembered, however, that it’s quite common for deer to leave a cornfield via a different trail than the one they used to enter the field, assuming, of course, that the deer are bedding somewhere other than in the corn itself. Therefore, a morning stand to intercept the deer leaving the corn will undoubtedly be in a different place than an evening stand that has been set up to ambush deer coming from their bedding areas to the corn.

Thus, what a hunter initially wants to do after locating trails is to ascertain what time of day they’re being used. The direction in which tracks are pointing is a sure clue — if the tracks are pointing toward the corn, they were probably made in the evening; if they are directed away from the corn, they probably indicate an exit trail that the animals use in the morning. Also, the hunter should be on the lookout for corncobs. Because deer obviously do not carry cobs from their bedding region back to the cornfield, but do carry cobs from the field to their bedding sites, the presence of intermittent cobs along the trail indicates in no uncertain terms that the travel route is a morning trail.

As a general rule, I do not like for either a morning stand or an evening stand to be too close to a cornfield where deer are feeding. If possible, depending upon his evaluation of the terrain, a hunter should try to situate his stands or blinds 100 to 200 yards from the cornfield so that he can overlook the exit and entrance trails that the deer are using to enter or leave the food plot.

It has been revealed that there are several good reasons for this strategy. To begin with, the largest bucks in any given region do not like to expose themselves unnecessarily in broad daylight, especially in regions where hunting pressure is intense. They can pretty much be counted upon to leave the cornfield at the very hint of early morning’s first light. Because it may still be too dark to shoot accurately, the hunter wants to be farther back down the trail that the deer are using so that by the time they reach the stand location, it will be fully light enough to see.

Industry observers note that conversely, in the evening hours, the very largest bucks seldom enter a cornfield when the sky is still brightly illuminated. They like to linger back in the shaded, heavy cover of their bedding areas, sometimes not actually entering the cornfield until after full dark. Naturally, therefore, if a stand or blind is positioned close to the cornfield, by the time the deer reach the location, it will be too dark to see.

According to recent reports, in all of this, it should be kept in mind that though the hunter doesn’t want to position his stand too close to the cornfield for either a morning or an evening watch, neither does he want his stand too close to the bedding area that the animals are using. This is simply too risky because the animals are very likely to detect the hunter as he tries to approach his stand site; and if they are spooked from the very region that they previously considered the safest place to be, they may not return for many days.

In fact, it’s worth mentioning that during the course of scouting, I always move slowly but make plenty of noise. Sometimes, I even whistle to myself as though I’m engaged in some type of routine outdoor work such as that of a surveyor or forester. Whitetails are accustomed to this type of minor disturbance, and they will simply circle around the intruder. And because the deer have the opportunity to hide or sneak away undetected, they’ll still have full confidence in the security of their chosen area, prompting them to return shortly after I’ve left.

Later, when I return to begin my hunting vigil, I stalk my stand. I actually sneak up on it just as though I were stillhunting through the woods. By doing this, the chances of any nearby deer recognizing my presence are much lower.

It has been revealed that pursuing whitetails when they’re actually in the corn is one of deer hunting’s most challenging and exciting endeavors. But the hunter should remember two things: If the terrain surrounding the cornfield is devoid of thick security cover, meaning that the corn itself is the very best place to hide and bed, the deer will probably cling to the corn all day and every day. This is especially the case if water is readily available in rain-filled puddles or tractor ruts. The second thing to remember — again — is that the windiest days are the best days to hunt.

Simply sneak-hunting around the perimeter of the cornfield can put venison on the meat pole, particularly during the early and late hours of the day, when the deer are feeding and have a tendency to work along “edges.” I’ve most often found this to be the case when the cornfield is bordered on one or more sides by lush hay meadows planted to some legume such as alfalfa, red or white clover or lespedeza. This is because it’s rather uncustomary for whitetails to gorge themselves on a single food type, as they are opportunists in their feeding habits and like variety in their diets. Therefore, if you know of a cornfield bordered by some other equally preferred food, you’ve hit paydirt!

Sources indicate that in sneak-hunting around the perimeter of a cornfield, a hunter shouldn’t expose himself in the open by remaining along the outside edge. Instead, he should stay one or two rows inside the edge of the cornfield — just far enough in so that he’s concealed yet can still see along the outside edge and into the adjacent, secondary food plot. The only exception to this rule is when the cornfield butts up directly against a brushy thicket or other bordering cover. In this case, the hunter can remain along the outermost edge of the corn and move slowly along with minimal chance of detection.

If the entire outside perimeter of the cornfield has been worked and no deer have been seen, it’s now time to assume that the whitetails are deeper within the confines of the corn, where they are most probably either feeding or bedding.

In a recent development, if the hunter is familiar with the terrain from previous scouting missions — before the corn was planted — he should try to recall the locations in the field where there were rock piles, soupy swales, sand pockets and the like. These exist in many fields, and farmers simply plow and plant around them. Once the surrounding corn has grown high, however, such places are hidden from view, and they are the very types of locations where deer commonly like to bed. The hunter should sneak up on these places during windy conditions, and he might very well shoot an unsuspecting deer right in its bed.

Industry observers note that if firearms are being used and several hunting partners are working together, staging drives is an excellent way to push deer through the corn to the opposite end of the field, where standers are likely to have shots. But there are a few vital points to bear in mind when using this method. If the cornfield is large, it is imperative that a large number of drivers — spaced no more than eight to 10 rows apart — be employed, because otherwise the deer, reluctant to leave the security of the cover, will tirelessly circle and sneak back between the drivers. Consequently, if there are only a few hunters participating in the drive, only smaller cornfields where the animals can be moved effectively in a predetermined direction should be hunted.

Also, in the interest of safety, drives in cornfields should ideally include stand hunters placed in tree stands, or at least on some other elevated vantage points such as hillsides or knolls. This way, they will be able to look down and through the rows of corn to see both the escaping deer and their approaching partners. Likewise, when they shoot from such higher locations, the angles of their shots will be acutely downward, rather than horizontal.

Bowhunters can also enact drives in cornfields, but instead of hunting parallel with the rows in an attempt to push deer to standers in the distance, they should hunt perpendicular to the rows. In this type of situation, no hunters need be placed on stand.

Along the edge of the cornfield, the bowhunters should be spaced about 100 yards apart. The team leader at one end of this drive line should then use his arm to signal the first hunter on the far end to enter the field. As this hunter enters the first row, he should look right and left, then move on to the second row, and so on. After about 30 seconds, the drive master should then motion the next hunter to enter the cornfield in the same manner. What results is that instead of a straight and even drive line moving through the field, there is a diagonal shift across the field. Therefore, if a hunter enters a row and sees a deer he wants to shoot at, he can do so to either his right or left with complete confidence in safety, knowing that his partners to either side are far ahead of or behind him. If he does not wish to shoot, the deer will usually run parallel to the rows and eventually offer a shot to one of the next hunters in the line.

Recent findings suggest that finally, one of the shrewdest ways I know to evaluate potential cornfield hunting situations, especially in unfamiliar regions, is to go to a local airport and hire a small plane to fly over the terrain. Most pilots charge an average of $30 per hour, and if two hunters split the expense, the cost per person is not prohibitive. But most crucial, in one hour of flying about 500 feet above the ground, a hunter can learn more about an area than he can in two weeks of driving back roads and scouting on foot. A topographic map should be brought along, and the location and configuration of every cornfield in the region should be marked. Adjacent terrain and cover should be carefully examined, and it then should be easy to determine with a high level of accuracy how deer are living, moving and feeding in each specific region.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

Believe me, if there are cornfields in the region you plan to hunt, you can be sure that bucks are in the corn — if not continuously, then at least intermittently. In either case, you should make the effort to be on hand, too, and when you leave, the chances are excellent that you’ll be dragging your deer behind you.

This story, “Deer By The Ear,” appeared in the November 1988 concern of Outdoor Life.

According to recent reports, oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare stated on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”).

It has been revealed that anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

Sources indicate that but tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:.

Sources indicate that kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

According to recent reports, it’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!).

Sources indicate that one-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he stated he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

According to recent reports, reflect in the Wild @ Lions Lair, a mirrored Catskills hideaway near Hunter Mountain. (Photo: Courtesy of Airbnb).

It has been revealed that I’ve planned most of my ski trips around one thing: the skiing. How’s the terrain? What’s the vert? How deep is the base? When’s the next storm?

According to recent reports, where I’m sleeping has generally been a secondary consideration. Give me a comfortable bed, a place to dry my gear, and a clean bathroom, and I’m happy.

In a recent development, but this holiday season, I’m dreaming bigger. What if, instead of the usual marathon of cooking, cleaning, and navigating family drama, we packed up our skis, gathered our favorite people, and disappeared into the mountains for a few days?

Of course, if I’m going to convince everyone to trade their usual holiday traditions for a ski trip, a cramped motel room and a communal boot dryer probably won’t cut it.

Sources indicate that A gorgeous cabin with a roaring fireplace, a proper kitchen for holiday dinners, and a hot tub waiting after last chair? Now we’re talking.

Apparently, I’m not the only one who likes the idea.

According to Airbnb’s latest winter travel report, travelers are increasingly looking to smaller mountain towns for their holiday getaways. Searches for holiday stays in Hunter, New York, are up 37 percent year over year, while ski destinations like Brian Head, Utah, and Mammoth Lakes, California, also made the organization’s list of trending winter escapes.

According to recent reports, and with Airbnb’s new checkout rules, which generally prohibit hosts from requiring guests to strip beds, start laundry, or wash and put away dishes for bookings made on or after November 20, what’s not to love? Sorry, family and friends, the same rules do not apply at Chalet de Shafer. Here’s a sponge.

From a sprawling Mammoth chalet that sleeps 12 to a romantic mirrored hideaway in the Catskills, these seven properties offer a compelling alternative to the usual holiday routine: beautiful mountain settings, plenty of character, inspiration to make a few new traditions, and, most importantly, nearby skiing.

Some ski trips are easy; others require a group chat, a shared grocery list, and a spreadsheet. This five-bedroom Mammoth Lakes townhouse was made for the latter.

Industry observers note that located near Canyon Lodge, the spacious retreat sleeps 12 and offers easy access to one of the West’s most impressive ski mountains. The townhouse puts skiers near several lifts, with access to beginner terrain, intermediate cruisers, and connections to Mammoth’s more challenging slopes. There’s also a free gondola connecting Canyon Lodge to the Village, making dinner and après intends a lot easier.

I’ve been on enough group ski trips to know that getting 12 people out the door at the same time is an unachievable goal. That’s why staying within walking distance of multiple lifts accessing Mammoth’s sprawling terrain is such a gift. Everyone can ski on their own schedule, and nobody has to organize a carpool.

Mammoth ranked No. 7 in the West in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and landed in the Top 10 for snow, grooming, and terrain variety. With more than 3,500 acres of skiable terrain, 3,100 feet of vertical, and a summit elevation above 11,000 feet, it’s the kind of mountain that can keep even the most ambitious skiers occupied for days.

According to recent reports, inside the townhouse, you’ll find a wood-burning fireplace, private steam room, arcade table, and a well-equipped kitchen designed to feed a crowd. There’s ski and gear storage, too, which anyone who has shared a vacation rental with 11 other skiers will appreciate.

And because the Canyon Lodge lifts are within walking distance, you can leave the cars parked and focus on the important stuff, like who forgot to buy coffee and whose turn it is to make breakfast.

New Yorkers don’t have to travel far to find a proper ski weekend. Hunter Mountain, about 2.5 hours from the city, offers 1,600 feet of vertical and some of the most substantial lift-served skiing in the Catskills. And while Western skiers might turn their noses up at skiing in New York, anyone who’s spent time on the East Coast knows there’s a particular satisfaction in making the most of whatever winter throws at you. Hunter’s extensive snowmaking helps with that.

Sources indicate that and just down the road is an architecturally stunning 225-square-foot mirrored tiny home that practically disappears into the surrounding forest. There’s a private wraparound deck with a hot tub, hammock, and outdoor fireplace, plus access to an all-glass sauna. It’s the kind of place that makes a romantic ski weekend feel considerably more romantic.

And if you’re a true New Yorker without a car, take a tip from my friend Abby and take the $59 round-trip ski bus from Manhattan to Hunter Mountain. You’ll still need to figure out transportation between the mountain and the cabin, but it’s a pretty compelling alternative to renting a car for the weekend. Check the bus schedule before planning an overnight stay.

This ski-town rental has one amenity that immediately caught our attention: a private sauna overlooking a Vermont river.

Located along the Brewster River near Smugglers’ Notch, this two-bedroom cottage is surrounded by 20 acres of mountain scenery. Large windows frame the water, while a wood-burning fire pit and sauna make post-ski recovery a major draw.

Industry observers note that the fully equipped kitchen and riverside dining area are ideal for slow mornings, though there’s plenty of reason to head out early. Just a short drive away, Smugglers’ Notch Resort spreads across three mountains, with 78 trails and plenty of tree skiing.

Smugglers’ Notch has a reputation as a family resort (it earned the No. 2 spot for family friendliness in our 2027 Resort Guide), which might lead you to imagine an endless procession of pizza wedges and children in matching ski-school vests. But over on Madonna and Sterling, the mountain has some legitimately challenging terrain, including steep trails and tree skiing that demand your full attention.

It has been revealed that smuggs ranked No. 11 in the East in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and earned the No. 3 spot for value and No. 5 for terrain variety. Not bad for a mountain that still feels refreshingly old-school. In other words, you can spend the day skiing some legitimately challenging terrain and the evening recovering in a sauna with a view, with absolutely no obligation to do anything productive.

One thing to know: The hosts require four-wheel or all-wheel drive for winter access, and Route 108 through Smugglers’ Notch Pass closes seasonally.

Some ski trip lodging is designed for little more than getting some sleep between ski days. Others feel like the main event.

The Cabin at Bear River, a 560-square-foot retreat tucked into 3.5 wooded acres near Sunday River, falls firmly into the second category.

The fireplace, radiant-heated floors, and well-equipped kitchen, complete with a fondue pot and KitchenAid mixer, make a compelling case for a particularly civilized après experience.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re ready to ski off that Gruyère, Sunday River is just down the road. Spanning eight interconnected peaks and 884 skiable acres, the Maine resort offers everything from long groomers to challenging steeps. Expert skiers can test themselves on White Heat, one of the East’s famously steep double-black-diamond runs, while intermediates will find plenty to explore across the mountain.

In a recent development, sunday River ranked No. 9 in the East in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and earned top-10 honors for grooming, lifts, and terrain variety.

Back at the cabin, there’s a private sauna and outdoor hot tub waiting. Call it recovery if you want. Personally, I don’t need a sports scientist to justify cranking those jets all the way up.

Sources indicate that utah’s ski reputation has been built largely on the Cottonwood Canyons, and for good reason. But there’s a whole other ski experience waiting four hours south of Salt Lake City, where the mountains look nothing like the Wasatch, the base elevation is a lofty 9,600 feet, and you don’t have to spend your morning sitting in the red snake of traffic wondering whether everyone else in the state also called in sick.

Brian Head Resort is one of Utah’s highest-elevation ski resorts. Its two mountains, Giant Steps and Navajo, offer 72 trails and 1,320 feet of vertical. Navajo is a good place for beginners to get their ski legs, while Giant Steps has more challenging terrain, including intermediate and expert runs and terrain parks.

The surrounding landscape is a world away from the Wasatch, too. Think high-desert scenery, red-rock country, and the chance to tack on a visit to nearby Cedar Breaks National Monument.

And tucked among the trees, just a short drive from the lifts, is this striking Scandinavian-inspired chalet that I think I might actually take off this list so I can have it all to myself. (Rapidly Googles “squatters’ rights in Utah.”).

Inside, expansive windows let in plenty of natural light, while the clean, modern interiors make an excellent case for doing very little after skiing beyond enjoying the private hot tub and fire pit right outside.

With room for eight guests, it’s a great option for a group trip, especially if your friends appreciate a good at-home après setup as much as fresh snow.

If your ideal winter vacation includes a wood-burning fireplace, a good book, and excellent Upcoming England skiing, let us introduce The Conscious Cabin.

This renovated 777-square-foot log cabin sits on three wooded acres in Fresh Hampshire’s White Mountains, less than 10 minutes from downtown North Conway.

Industry observers note that inside, exposed timber and cozy furnishings deliver exactly the kind of atmosphere you’d hope for from a Fresh England cabin. Outside, there’s a spacious backyard with a fire pit, gazebo, and a short trail leading to a brook.

Nearby Cranmore Mountain, just outside downtown North Conway, offers 1,200 feet of vertical and 60 trails, and is particularly well suited to families and skiers who appreciate cruising groomers. For more challenging terrain, head to Attitash, where two peaks offer more than 300 skiable acres, including classic Fresh England trails, glades, and steeper runs.

In a recent development, both resorts made SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide, ranking No. 17 and No. 19 in the East, respectively. Cranmore also took the top spot for lodging and ranked No. 4 for dining, making North Conway an especially appealing base for a winter getaway.

After all, this charming cabin is considerably more appealing than spending the holidays sleeping on your aunt’s pullout couch in the basement.

If your ideal ski vacation includes a little European charm without the transatlantic flight, Mont-Tremblant makes a pretty convincing case.

The Québec resort is known for its colorful pedestrian village, lively après scene, and some of the most substantial lift-served skiing in Eastern Canada.

In a recent development, with more than 100 trails spread across four mountain faces, 763 skiable acres, and 2,116 feet of vertical, Tremblant has enough terrain to keep everyone from beginners to expert skiers entertained. Its extensive snowmaking system is another welcome advantage for early-season trips.

Perched on the mountainside, Horizon 115-204 is a modern three-bedroom condo with ski-in/ski-out access, so you can go from breakfast to the slopes without a complicated transportation plan.

It has been revealed that inside, there’s a gas fireplace, a fully equipped kitchen, and enough room for eight guests. A balcony offers mountain air and space for a post-ski drink, while an on-site hot tub gives you another great reason to get out of your ski boots promptly.

And if you’re not quite ready to call it a night, the resort’s pedestrian village is accessible by shuttle, with restaurants, bars, and enough après activity to keep the evening going.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect.
  • In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson).

Industry observers note that norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

According to recent reports, as someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

According to recent reports, I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

If you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

Industry observers note that I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, Latest Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

In a recent development, the “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

According to recent reports, norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.

A Routine Invasive-Species Survey in Lake Ontario Turned Up Something Much Stranger

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.
  • Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week.
  • Industry observers note that “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.

Industry observers note that A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week. The fish came from Oswego Harbor, Newly introduced York, which is on the southeastern side of Lake Ontario. It’s a significant find for more than just its color variation.

Industry observers note that “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov. 10. “The species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor.”.

In a recent development, running the full length of an arm, the off-colored native burbot had xanthochromism, a genetic mutation that causes an animal’s pigment to be excessively yellow or orange. In fish, it displays on their scales and fins, but it can also show up on furred animals. It’s less common than albinism in the wild, but it’s also not unheard of.

A 6.6-foot orange-Creamsicle nurse shark turned up with the same condition, plus albinism, in 2024 in Costa Rica, and the first case of xanthochromism in a sunset-colored snook in the Gulf was documented in 2024.

The variation might be appealing to fishermen, but it’s less fun for the fish themselves. Their bold coloring reduces their ability to hide within their habitat, which means they’re easy prey and often have shorter lifespans.

The deadly-bright hues look similar to banana trout, but that’s a different scenario.

It has been revealed that palomino trout, or bananas, are popular stockers for pond practice. They’re also covered in shades ranging from yellow to orange, but they’re bred that way on purpose. Hatcheries breed them from a mutant rainbow trout strain that lacks the dot pattern but keeps the bow’s notorious red lateral stripe. Despite the golden color, they aren’t related to California golden trout. The strain traces to a single yellow-mottled rainbow fingerling found at a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 and was introduced to anglers in 1963.

Industry observers note that as for the yellow burbot in Oswego, it wasn’t released.
